The district then needs to know how many of the 300 non-visitors chose to forgo the allotment, collected elsewhere, or could not get to the shop. National Food Security Act, section 3

There is also a distributional reason to track delays separately from final collection. A household that finally receives two months of grain together may have borrowed or paid retail prices to bridge the first month. Recording only the eventual quantity treats the household as fully served while missing the cost of that gap. A short household survey can ask how long people went without their allocation and how they replaced it. Combined with the verified delivery record, that makes it possible to tell whether a district is improving access or simply clearing arrears.

Portability makes that investigation more important. A migrant household that collects grain in another district should count as served even though its original shop has no transaction. Conversely, a household with a broken record can disappear from the transaction denominator altogether. The denominator should start from the entitlement roll, reconcile verified portable claims and then use a sample of households to check what happened to the rest. Publishing both the verified delivery rate and the share of cases with an unresolved outcome would be more informative than quietly treating every missing record as either fraud or voluntary non-use.

Stricter identification can reduce diversion and increase exclusion

The strongest case for stricter authentication is that it raises the cost of collecting grain in someone else’s name or entering a sale that never took place. The relevant Indian evidence also shows the price of transition failures. Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar studied biometric identity requirements in Jharkhand’s ration system and found a reduction in corruption alongside significant disruption to legitimate access. Their analysis attributed much of the adverse effect to how the transition was managed. An estimate from Jharkhand cannot simply be carried over to every state. It does show that enforcement rules and exception handling can change the result of adopting the same technology. Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar’s Jharkhand study

A workable fallback would let a documented eligible customer collect grain when connectivity or the usual authentication method fails, while recording the reason and retaining a trail for later review. Automatic rejection would place the cost of a technical fault on the household. An untracked override would move the risk to the public ledger. Sampling repeated overrides, large adjustments and duplicate claims after reconciliation offers a way to keep access open without overlooking these patterns. It should also be possible for a person who was refused grain to record a complaint without going through the dealer who refused it.

What would justify expanding the reforms

States should compare independently verified delivery, wrongful denial, stock discrepancies and collection costs across comparable groups of shops. A phased introduction gives a stronger comparison than a single national before-and-after figure, particularly when harvest conditions and grain allocations are changing at the same time. The sample should include people who did not transact and shops in low-connectivity areas. Interviews should record actual kilograms received and the cost of repeat visits. When possible, field staff can check a sample of transactions against household reports and physical stock records.

There is a strong case for expanding measures that cut independently measured diversion without increasing denial, travel costs or repeat visits. If reconciliation improves while household collection falls, the next rupee should address the point of failure. It could be timely movement of stock, a dependable offline process or a more viable shop in a remote area. The Cabinet has put those spending decisions in the same programme. A common measure of actual household receipts would let states compare what each can deliver. Cabinet decision on SARTHAK-PDS

excerpt.rendered: India’s SARTHAK-PDS scheme puts logistics, ration-shop incentives and authentication in one programme. Its test is how much grain eligible households actually take home.

title.rendered: India’s kharif support prices matter most where farmers can sell at them

content.rendered:
India can use its kharif support prices to encourage a wider mix of crops, but an increase on paper will change planting only if growers expect to sell on those terms. On 13 May the government raised the minimum support prices for 14 kharif crops for the 2026–27 marketing season. Common paddy rises from ₹2,369 to ₹2,441 a quintal. Tur rises from ₹8,000 to ₹8,450, while maize rises by only ₹10 to ₹2,410. The difference in announced increases is relevant to planting. The likelihood of procurement, the price paid by private buyers, yield risk and cash costs can matter more than the change in the schedule. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices · Business Standard’s coverage of the kharif decision

What a support price can do before a crop is planted

A support price can give farmers a credible minimum return when procurement is accessible and buyers know the agency will purchase the crop at the announced price. Where purchase centres are distant, quantities are limited, payments are slow or the crop fails quality tests, the published figure is a weaker guide to the cash a farmer receives. The same headline price can have a large effect in a district with dependable procurement and a modest one in a district where farmers mostly sell to private traders. This is especially important when comparing paddy with alternatives. A farmer can be willing to switch and still keep growing the crop for which collection and payment are predictable. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices · Department of Food and Public Distribution’s December 2025 bulletin

The government’s price table reports an estimated common paddy cost of ₹1,627 per quintal and a new MSP of ₹2,441, about 50% higher on that measure. Tur’s estimated cost is ₹5,496 and its new MSP is ₹8,450, a reported margin of 54%. These are national cost estimates and the margin is calculated against the cost definition in the official table. Neither figure is a household’s expected profit. Local yields, irrigation, rents, family labour and borrowing costs can vary. Even a farmer who produces at the estimated cost may sell only part of the crop at the support price. The budget for a crop decision needs revenue and cost per acre, with realistic prices for the saleable output. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices

Consider two illustrative marketing situations for tur. In the first, a grower sells ten quintals, all at ₹8,450, for revenue of ₹84,500. In the second, only half is purchased at MSP and the rest is sold at a hypothetical ₹7,400 per quintal. Revenue falls to ₹79,250 before transport, grading and finance costs. That ₹5,250 difference exceeds the ₹4,500 gain the announced ₹450 increase would have delivered across all ten quintals. These are scenarios, not crop-income estimates. They show why a higher probability of selling at the announced price can matter more than another increase in the price itself. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices

The size of the revision varies across substitutes. The paddy increase is about 3.0 per cent, against 5.6 per cent for tur. Moong, another pulse, rises by ₹12 to ₹8,780, and maize by ₹10 to ₹2,410. The effective price signal also depends on the cost benchmark. The Cabinet’s national cost estimates include paid-out expenses and imputed family labour. They do not add the rental value of owned land as a separate cost. A positive margin on that benchmark can coexist with a weak return on a tenant’s actual lease or with a stronger return from putting the same plot under a different crop. Where land and water are scarce, expected returns per hectare and per unit of irrigation give a better guide to planting than margins per quintal. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices

The procurement system shapes crop choices and public costs

Public procurement of paddy helps supply the food distribution system and gives farmers a reliable buyer in areas where procurement is active. The same system can make it harder to diversify if an alternative crop lacks local traders, storage or predictable quality standards. A farmer considering pulses or oilseeds also has to account for differences in yield volatility and the timing of payments. If the private market remains shallow, a higher MSP may primarily raise expectations at the start of the season. Changing acreage requires a credible plan for who buys the produce when farmers start selling at the same time. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices · Department of Food and Public Distribution’s December 2025 bulletin

There is a strong case for expanding procurement where a region would benefit from more diverse production and private buying has not developed. A limited purchase commitment can attract processors and reduce a farmer’s downside during the first seasons of a switch. The fiscal case weakens if public buying becomes the only reliable outlet or the government must finance and dispose of stocks indefinitely. Procurement raises handling, transport and storage costs, and the value of the stocks depends on what the public sector can do with them. Pilot commitments linked to a specific region, crop and marketing window would reveal more about additional acreage and private demand than a nationwide volume target alone.

Where the policy objective is income support and the government has no corresponding stock requirement, a price deficiency payment is worth testing. With an independently verified market reference of ₹7,600 and a tur MSP of ₹8,450, compensating the full gap on ten eligible quintals would cost ₹8,500. It would avoid buying and storing those ten quintals, though it would introduce different risks. If local traders can coordinate bids or sellers can report fictional transactions, the payment may subsidise depressed prices or claims without grain. Verified sales, competitive bidding and a benchmark that cannot be moved easily by one mandi matter more to the design than reimbursing every quoted shortfall.

Water use is another reason to distinguish the policy objectives. Paddy can provide dependable income in a well-developed procurement region, while water-intensive production may impose costs on other users or on the state budget where pumping is subsidised. An alternative crop’s value then includes the resources it saves as well as the revenue it brings the grower. A higher support price for the alternative addresses only one part of that comparison. Reliable seeds, suitable agronomy, storage and a market for the crop can be decisive. A policy that pays farmers to take on a new risk should make the complementary investments visible rather than assuming a price signal will provide them. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices · Business Standard’s coverage of the kharif decision

Measure realised prices and the reasons farmers still choose paddy

Compare mandi and farm-gate prices with MSP for comparable grades, alongside the share of marketable surplus procured, distance to purchase centres and time to receive payment. Break the figures down by state and farm size. A small farmer who has to sell quickly can face worse terms than a larger farmer able to store, grade or transport a crop. If rising pulse and oilseed MSPs coincide with higher realised prices, new buyers and sustained acreage in suitable regions, the case for the policy strengthens. If most of the gain accrues to producers already selling through established procurement and alternative crops remain difficult to market, improving access would do more than another broad price increase. Cabinet decision on the 2026–27 kharif support prices · Department of Food and Public Distribution’s December 2025 bulletin

The next test comes when crops arrive. Assess public costs alongside changes in prices and production, including how much stock was bought, what it cost to handle and whether it found a durable use. Also compare what farmers would have planted under similar rainfall and input prices without the change. Planting decisions respond to the monsoon and to last season’s prices, so an increase in acreage alone cannot identify the effect of MSP. The purpose of a price floor is to make farming income more reliable. That is best measured through the terms growers actually receive and the options they can credibly choose.

excerpt.rendered: The new support prices favour several pulses and oilseeds on paper. Farmers will compare the prices they can actually realise after allowing for procurement, yield risk and the cost of switching crops.

title.rendered: Pakistan’s power reform should be judged by the arrears it prevents

content.rendered:
Pakistan’s electricity-sector repair will be durable when it stops generating obligations the power system cannot pay. The IMF’s May review gives a basis for asking whether the decline in the measured stock of circular debt reflects better operating cash flows or a change in how past obligations are financed. Clearing arrears can help suppliers operate and reduce immediate financing pressure. If the cost of generating and delivering electricity still exceeds cash collected and predictable public support, the gap can return even after a large settlement. IMF’s May Board decision for Pakistan · IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

The liability can change hands without the gap disappearing

Circular debt describes unpaid obligations that accumulate as cash shortfalls move through the electricity chain. A distributor that receives less cash than it owes upstream can delay payments. The supplier may in turn owe fuel providers or creditors. These obligations can affect reliability and the willingness of firms to provide working capital. The IMF staff report separates the flow of new circular debt and the clearance of payment arrears when describing changes in the stock. A reduction in the stock can result from a settlement even in a period when operations continue to produce new arrears. IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

For example, suppose unpaid obligations begin at 200 units. A financing operation clears 60 during the year, while the power system adds 25 in new arrears. The measured stock falls to 165, a decline of 35. The operating gap is still 25. If the settlement used borrowing backed by the government, some of the obligation may now sit elsewhere on the public balance sheet. This is stylised arithmetic. It shows why an audit should track both annual additions and liabilities elsewhere after refinancing. A lower stock can be valuable while giving an incomplete measure of reform.

The monthly cash calculation starts with energy delivered, the amount billed, the share actually paid and any public support received. Physical losses reduce billable energy. Billing problems reduce what is charged for it. Collection problems reduce the cash received. Delayed government payments can create a cash gap even where a tariff or subsidy is intended to cover costs on paper. These causes call for different responses. A general tariff increase changes the amount billed to customers already in the system. It cannot directly recover electricity lost in the network or make an overdue government payment arrive on time. IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

The tariff dilemma is about incentives and distribution

Higher prices may be necessary where costs have persistently exceeded receipts. A household with few substitutes can have little room to adjust essential consumption, while an industrial customer may reduce use or look for self-supply. If a distributor loses customers that pay reliably, it can struggle to cover fixed network costs even after a tariff increase. The strength of this effect depends on who can leave the system, what charges remain due and how the tariff is structured. A financial forecast should account for collection and demand responses under alternative prices. It should also identify how lower-income consumers receive support and when the utility is reimbursed. IMF’s May Board decision for Pakistan · IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

A more targeted subsidy can reduce the strain on the budget where it directs support towards essential consumption and vulnerable users. Targeting has administrative costs and can exclude people whose accounts or eligibility are hard to establish. An explicit budget payment gives the finance ministry and legislature a way to see the cost, while missed reimbursements should be reported as arrears. This improves accountability for decisions that otherwise appear as losses at the utility. It does not eliminate the need to track access and disconnections, particularly where several families share a connection.

Why clearing past arrears can still be justified

The strongest case for a settlement is that legacy debts can prevent efficient firms from operating and amplify the cost of financing fuel and repairs. A credible clearance can lower those costs and improve near-term reliability. It should be evaluated against an alternative in which suppliers remain unpaid, not just against a world with no legacy debt. The condition is that settlement be paired with measures to change the flow of new obligations. Otherwise creditors may reasonably expect another settlement, and taxpayers can end up financing recurring losses at a different point in the chain. IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

External shocks complicate the test. Imported fuel costs or currency changes can increase the cost of power before prices or transfers adjust. A durable approach needs a transparent way to allocate those shocks across consumers, firms and the budget, with payment schedules the parties can meet. It should also show when an increase in costs is temporary and when it changes the long-run economics of a plant or contract. A system that can cover current bills only in unusually favourable conditions remains exposed after the legacy stock falls. IMF’s May Board decision for Pakistan

Creditors also care about whether a new liability has better terms. Replacing a short overdue payable with longer debt can reduce immediate pressure and make the schedule more transparent. It can still increase total interest or move repayment to a government entity with limited own revenue. The settlement should disclose its maturity, rate and source of repayment so its value can be compared with the old obligation. That comparison also gives taxpayers a way to see which part of the improvement comes from better finance and which from stronger operations. IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

The next review should show the cash flow

Follow new arrears, settlements, subsidy reimbursements, network losses, collections and reliability in a common reporting period. Reconcile changes in the sector’s debt with any new obligations elsewhere in government. If arrears creation slows while the system continues delivering power and eligible households can still afford it, the reform has improved the underlying economics. If headline debt falls while unpaid obligations resume or budget support becomes less visible, the next review will need to identify where the gap moved. The result matters for the fiscal position as well as for the firms and households buying power. IMF’s May Board decision for Pakistan · IMF’s May staff report on Pakistan, including the power-sector debt table

excerpt.rendered: The IMF’s latest review separates changes in the stock of electricity-sector debt from the flow of new arrears. That distinction matters for prices, reliability and the budget.

title.rendered: India’s higher gold duty faces a test in tonnes, premiums and recycling

content.rendered:
India’s increase in gold and silver import duties can help the external account if it changes how much metal the country buys abroad. A higher domestic price is only the first step. From 13 May the effective rate on standard gold and silver imports rose from 6% to 15%, with separate treatment for some other precious-metal products. The government says it wants to conserve foreign exchange amid the West Asia disruption. The policy should be judged by changes in physical net imports and the sources of domestic supply. Customs revenue, retail prices and foreign-exchange savings can move in different directions. DD News on the May customs changes · Reuters on the new import duties · CBIC basic customs duty notification

Nine points on the tax rate translates to an 8.5% change in the import price

Suppose an importer buys standard gold with a customs value of ₹100 before the relevant duty, and the world price and exchange rate stay fixed. The duty-inclusive cost rises from ₹106 to ₹115, about 8.5%. This excludes other taxes and costs and assumes the full duty applies. Local wholesale and retail prices need not rise by the same amount. Dealers can sell stocks bought under the earlier rate. Households can offer existing holdings for sale. Importers and jewellers may also absorb some of the increase in their margins where demand is weak. An import-price calculation is a benchmark for identifying those adjustments. DD News on the May customs changes · Reuters on the new import duties

Contemporaneous reporting put India’s 2025–26 gold imports at about $72 billion in value. The size of that bill makes the policy material, but a dollar value combines tonnage with the world price. If the world price rises enough, India can import fewer tonnes and still pay more dollars than before. Conversely, a decline in import value caused by a lower world price says little about whether the duty changed demand. Compare volumes and unit values and distinguish an abrupt change in arrivals from a sustained one. Stocks landed before the tax change can cover demand for a time and make the initial fall in legal imports look larger. Business Standard on FY2025–26 gold imports · Reuters on the new import duties

That distinction is visible in the prior-year comparison. The $71.98 billion figure was about 24% higher than a year earlier, and reporting on the Commerce Ministry data attributed much of the increase to high gold prices. A government seeking to reduce dollar outflows therefore has to allow for prices set outside India. It should publish the change in volume and the contribution from unit values, with a separate line for changes in purity and product mix where possible. An unchanged import bill could still represent policy-induced restraint if it would have risen with the world price in the absence of the duty. That claim needs an explicit comparison, rather than treating the bill itself as the effect. Business Standard on FY2025–26 gold imports

A second example separates revenue from the external account. Suppose legally imported gold has an aggregate customs value of $100 million at the old rate and $90 million at the new one because physical purchases fall 10% at an unchanged world price. The import bill falls by $10 million. The duty rises from the rupee equivalent of $6 million to $13.5 million, holding the exchange rate and the duty base definition fixed. These are illustrative amounts. Higher tax revenue can therefore accompany lower foreign-exchange demand. If imports are replaced with unrecorded purchases abroad, the recorded bill may fall without an equivalent reduction in the country’s underlying demand for foreign currency.

Recycling is one way the adjustment can work

Gold held by households is a large potential source of metal. When the domestic price rises relative to other uses of savings, some households may sell old jewellery, bars or coins. Recycled metal can meet part of jewellers’ demand without requiring a new import. Reuters reported that the price move prompted some domestic selling and that dealer discounts against official prices widened sharply. That is a contemporaneous observation, not a national quantity estimate. If the discount persists and recycled volumes rise through formal channels, the evidence for substitution becomes stronger. If discounts disappear after old stocks run down and demand returns, the initial change may have been mostly timing. Reuters on domestic discounts and selling

The distribution is uneven. Existing holders can receive a higher local price if they choose to sell. A household buying jewellery for a fixed date may face a higher bill and have little immediate room to delay. A jeweller financing inventory has to tie up more rupees for the same amount of metal. Larger firms may be better able to fund the difference or source recycled material. Smaller shops can face a squeeze if customers resist higher prices and suppliers want payment sooner. An exporter competing at a world price may have even less ability to pass on a domestic input premium, which is why the rules governing export-linked inputs matter separately from the headline rate. DD News on the May customs changes · Reuters on the new import duties

The government also moved on 14 May to cap duty-free gold imports for jewellery exports under advance authorisation at 100 kilograms per licence, according to Reuters. That measure has a separate purpose and a different denominator from the domestic duty. It seeks to contain the use of a concession while allowing inputs for export. If a firm can import only in smaller lots, verification may become easier but the cost of repeated approvals and financing can rise. Compare the gold bought under the concession with the value and physical content of verified exports. Tighter administration is more likely to help when it targets unexplained gaps between the two, with timely clearance for firms that meet the rules. Reuters on the advance authorisation cap · DGFT’s rules for gems and jewellery exporters

The strongest case is for temporary relief in a stressed external account

The import duty raises the relative price of a purchase that some households and firms can postpone. That makes it a faster instrument than many policies that would improve the external account over several years. It can be defensible during a short disruption if it reduces the need for other adjustments. The strongest objection is that gold demand reflects long-standing saving and consumption preferences. If households still want to acquire metal, a wider gap with foreign prices can change the route by which it arrives. A large and persistent premium can reward diversion and penalise compliant businesses. Enforcement and reporting can reduce the problem, but the cost of maintaining a wide wedge rises if the policy has little effect on final demand. DD News on the May customs changes · Reuters on domestic discounts and selling

A better assessment would distinguish purchases of newly imported metal, locally recycled material and investment products that change the form of household exposure. A switch from jewellery to a financial claim backed by newly purchased physical gold can still require imports. A switch into an investment with no additional purchase of metal has a different effect. This distinction matters if the policy objective is the net demand for foreign currency rather than the pattern of retail buying. It also explains why a rise in formal financial products is not sufficient evidence that the import measure worked. Look at what the product issuer and the rest of the market bought to provide it.

What would make the policy worth its cost

Publish gold and silver import tonnage and value alongside wholesale premiums or discounts, recycling volumes, jewellery export performance and changes in customs enforcement. Compare those figures with earlier periods that had similar global prices and seasonal demand. If physical net imports fall for several months, legal recycled supply expands and export orders hold up, the case that the higher duty bought external relief strengthens. If recorded imports fall while premiums and unrecorded supply rise and exporters lose orders, a longer-lived duty deserves more scrutiny. The policy succeeds when India buys less new metal abroad at an acceptable cost to households and businesses that use it. DD News on the May customs changes · Business Standard on FY2025–26 gold imports

excerpt.rendered: The move from 6% to 15% can reduce foreign-exchange demand if it lowers net imports. The effects on local prices, recycled supply and jewellery exporters will determine how much it achieves.

title.rendered: India’s health financing needs to count the cost of ordinary visits

content.rendered:
A health-financing policy can protect families from a large hospital bill and still leave them paying substantial amounts over repeated ordinary visits. India’s National Health Accounts put out-of-pocket spending at 39.4 per cent of total health expenditure in 2021–22, down from 64.2 per cent in 2013–14. That is an important change in who finances health spending. It does not measure the share of households protected against high costs or identify which treatment they can afford to obtain. The next question is what primary care can do to reduce recurring payments and the cost of reaching a usable service. Health ministry’s National Health Accounts release · PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants

The denominator tells only part of the story

The share of spending paid out of pocket can fall because household payments fall, because government or other spending rises, or through a combination. It is also calculated across people who face different health needs and access. PRS reports out-of-pocket spending at 45 per cent of current health expenditure in 2021–22, a measure that excludes capital expenditure and therefore has a different denominator from the 39.4 per cent figure. Neither ratio shows whether the same people are being treated or whether a household forgoes care when it cannot pay. Health ministry’s National Health Accounts release · PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants

The difference matters when comparing reforms. Expanding hospital cover can reduce the risk of a rare, expensive event. Providing reliable medicines and diagnostics in primary care can reduce a smaller cost incurred repeatedly. Assume a household faces six outpatient visits in a year, each costing ₹350 for medicines, ₹250 for tests and ₹150 for transport. That totals ₹4,500 before time away from work. If an accessible public facility covers the medicine and test costs on four of those visits, the assumed saving is ₹2,400 even if transport stays the same. These are illustrative amounts, not national averages or promised benefits.

Free on paper can still be expensive to use

A household may need another trip if a facility is closed, a medicine is unavailable or the relevant worker is absent. The cost can include wages forgone, childcare and transport as well as the eventual payment. When people cannot predict whether a visit will succeed, they may choose a more expensive private option or delay the visit. Assessing financial protection therefore requires measuring the availability and reliability of services. The Indian Public Health Standards provide a benchmark for facilities. The value of meeting a standard has to be checked against what people can actually obtain. Health ministry’s parliamentary reply on public health standards · PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants

There is also an equity effect. A salaried worker with paid leave may bear less of a financial penalty for a repeat visit than a person paid by the day. A household far from a diagnostic centre may spend more getting to the test than buying it. Looking only at the formal fee would miss those costs. Compare the total cost per resolved episode across locations and income groups, including people who report a need and never make a visit. Otherwise falling spending can be mistaken for financial protection when some people have simply stopped seeking care.

The case for focusing first on catastrophic bills

The strongest argument for prioritising hospital protection is that a single serious admission can exceed years of ordinary visit costs and force a family to borrow or sell assets. Pooling that risk can have a large welfare benefit. The case for strengthening primary care sits alongside it. Reliable first contact and access to routine services address a different part of household spending, and can help people reach further treatment when they need it. A budget decision should show how the marginal rupee changes spending, access or outcomes in each setting. A single financing share cannot settle the allocation. Health ministry’s National Health Accounts release · PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants

For the provider, staffing and supply chains are recurring obligations. An allocation for a building or new equipment cannot ensure a test is available six months later. A performance comparison should distinguish spending on assets from funds to operate them, and show whether they are used at the planned level. A facility that serves more patients reliably may cost more in the budget while saving households repeated private payments and time. Those effects belong in the same evaluation, with the impact on quality and unmet need reported explicitly. Health ministry’s parliamentary reply on public health standards · PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants

A financing decision can also change where patients are treated. If a first-contact provider cannot supply a basic service, patients may travel to a higher-level hospital or use another provider. That raises costs for the household and can draw staff time away from patients who need specialist care. An evaluation should follow the patient across facilities so that a low cost at one site does not simply reappear as a bill or waiting time elsewhere. A completed referral and a resolved episode are stronger outcomes than a facility visit in isolation. Health ministry’s parliamentary reply on public health standards

There is a reason to report the distribution of payments as well as their mean. A reduction in ordinary costs for many families can leave a smaller group still facing serious hardship, while a policy protecting the largest admissions may do little for widespread smaller costs. A budget can legitimately pursue both objectives. It needs evidence on who receives the protection and who continues to pay, particularly in areas with few alternatives. PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants

A more informative financial protection test

Track what patients pay for medicines, tests and travel, how many visits are needed, what care was forgone and whether access differs by household income or location. Connect those observations to facility operating hours and supplies. Compare changes for similar populations where service improvements arrive at different times, allowing for changes in local costs and demand. An improvement is convincing if households with a comparable need can get the service more predictably while paying less out of pocket. That evidence would show what a lower national spending share means in everyday care. Health ministry’s National Health Accounts release · PRS analysis of the 2026–27 health grants · Health ministry’s parliamentary reply on public health standards

excerpt.rendered: Hospital protection matters. So do repeated costs for medicines, tests, transport and lost work when primary care is hard to use.

title.rendered: India’s airline loan guarantees need a route-level test

content.rendered:
India has a case for helping airlines bridge a temporary shock to fuel and operating costs. The case is strongest when a loan keeps an otherwise viable route open and can be repaid from ordinary revenue once the disruption eases. The Cabinet’s 5 May approval of Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 5.0 targets ₹2.55 lakh crore of additional credit, including ₹5,000 crore for airlines. Those are lending targets. The government is taking on a contingent liability rather than spending those amounts immediately. An airline guarantee should be judged by the connectivity and competition that disappear without it, as well as by the risk that the loan merely delays a restructuring. Cabinet approval of ECLGS 5.0 · Civil Aviation Ministry on the airline guarantee · Reuters, 5 May

The guarantee changes the lender’s loss before it changes the airline’s economics

The Cabinet says lenders can receive 90% coverage of the amount in default for eligible airlines and other non-MSMEs, and 100% for eligible MSMEs. Scheduled passenger airlines must have qualifying outstanding credit facilities as of 31 March and standard accounts. Their additional credit can be up to 100% of the specified working-capital measure, subject to conditions and a cap of ₹1,500 crore per borrower. The loan term can run seven years with a two-year moratorium, against five years and a one-year moratorium for other eligible businesses. The moratorium changes when cash is due. The borrower still has to generate enough cash to repay. Cabinet approval of ECLGS 5.0

For illustration, suppose an eligible airline draws ₹500 crore and the entire principal is later outstanding when it defaults. If eventual recoveries cover ₹200 crore, the remaining net principal loss is ₹300 crore. A stylised allocation of that net loss at 90% would leave ₹270 crore with the guarantor and ₹30 crore with the lender. Actual payment and recovery timing, eligible amounts and sharing rules depend on the scheme’s terms. This is a sensitivity calculation, not a claim forecast. It shows why the fiscal exposure cannot be inferred from the loan target alone. The distribution of defaults, recoveries and outstanding balances will determine how much of the liability crystallises. Cabinet approval of ECLGS 5.0

A lender with only a small share of the downside can approve a loan it would otherwise reject. That is part of the point in a liquidity shock. The lender may be protecting its own short-term cash while a solvent airline is forced to cancel services. A public guarantee can correct that mismatch. The same mechanism can weaken scrutiny if a carrier’s expected revenue will not cover its costs even when fuel and routes normalise. Standard loan status on one date is a useful eligibility screen and an incomplete viability test. A lender should still ask where the airline will earn the cash to make repayments after the moratorium. Cabinet approval of ECLGS 5.0

The public benefit depends on which flights would be lost

The best argument for treating airlines differently is that an abrupt withdrawal of service can impose costs beyond the airline. Some passengers can switch to another carrier or use rail. For an airport with few flights, losing a regular connection can make a business trip or urgent journey much longer. An airline’s financial return from a flight may miss some of those benefits. A temporary loan can keep aircraft, staff and slots available while disruption passes, avoiding the cost of rebuilding the service. That argument is strongest where capacity would otherwise disappear and another operator cannot replace it quickly. Civil Aviation Ministry on the airline guarantee · Reuters, 5 May

The counterargument is that a guarantee granted to an incumbent can entrench its position, particularly if rivals already face difficulty obtaining slots or aircraft. Protecting an airline’s market share may do little for passengers if competitors could maintain the same routes and keep fares competitive. A lender that values the borrower’s whole balance sheet may also direct the money toward services that offer little distinctive public benefit. Where connectivity is the reason for support, record whether the money preserved seats on routes with few alternatives, how long that service lasted, and what happened to frequency and fares. These are better measures than the borrower’s total number of flights.

The national baseline makes this worth testing. In a 30 March parliamentary answer, the Ministry of Civil Aviation reported January domestic market shares of 63.6% for IndiGo and 26.5% for Air India, or 90.1% combined on those reported categories. A national share cannot establish that a particular city pair is uncompetitive. A route with several flights and a usable rail alternative can have more competitive discipline than the national total suggests. A smaller route may depend on a single carrier even if the national share of that carrier is low. Guarantee decisions can take advantage of this distinction by asking where seat supply actually falls, which alternatives passengers use, and whether a rival had a realistic opportunity to enter. A public programme that leaves route-level competition stronger can justify a fiscal cost that would be harder to defend if the benefit were simply preserving incumbent market shares. Civil Aviation Ministry’s parliamentary answer, 30 March · Civil Aviation Ministry on the airline guarantee

A useful stress test separates a temporary spike in the cost of flying from a permanent reduction in the viability of a route. Model the airline’s receipts under several combinations of load factor, fares and operating costs. An illustration shows the leverage. If a flight with 180 seats and an average fare of ₹6,000 goes from 85% occupancy to 75%, ticket revenue falls by ₹1.08 lakh per flight before ancillary revenue and taxes. Some of the operating cost remains even when seats are empty. If the route returns to a profitable load factor after the disruption, a bridge can make sense. If it needs permanently higher fares that passengers are unlikely to pay, more debt is a poor substitute for adjusting capacity.

Keep the measure temporary and assess whether lending is additional

A credible evaluation should track new guaranteed loans against ordinary lending to similar businesses. Otherwise a bank may move a facility it intended to offer anyway onto the government’s guarantee, shifting risk without expanding credit. For airlines, disclosure at an aggregate level should include the capacity preserved, borrowers’ repayment progress after the moratorium, eventual defaults and recoveries, and the size of the largest exposures. For smaller businesses, report how much additional working capital reached firms that could document orders or operating needs. The available guarantee may be most valuable where commercial credit tightened suddenly, and least valuable where it simply replaces a credit line already likely to be renewed. Cabinet approval of ECLGS 5.0

There is also a trade-off between broad support and simpler alternatives. If the objective is to preserve a small set of essential routes, transparent procurement of temporary service may cost less than insuring an entire carrier’s balance sheet. If the shock affects otherwise healthy airlines across many routes and the market is still competitive, a broadly available short-term credit backstop may work faster. The choice turns on whether the public benefit is network-wide or concentrated, and on whether the carrier can absorb the eventual costs from normal operations. The longer the guarantee lasts, the more important that distinction becomes.

The scheme earns its keep if guaranteed borrowers maintain service through the shock, private lenders resume carrying risk as conditions improve, and actual losses are small relative to the capacity preserved. The case weakens if disbursement grows while routes remain thin, fares rise because competition weakens, and borrowers need further support after the moratorium. The Cabinet announcement creates a means of financing a temporary disruption. It should be evaluated against the services that would otherwise have been lost and the eventual claims paid by the public guarantor. Cabinet approval of ECLGS 5.0 · Civil Aviation Ministry on the airline guarantee

excerpt.rendered: Emergency credit can keep airlines operating through a temporary cost shock. The public return depends on which services are preserved and whether carriers can repay once conditions normalise.

title.rendered: India’s expected-loss rules will make bank judgement more visible

content.rendered:
The RBI’s expected-credit-loss framework will bring more of a bank’s judgement about future losses into its accounts. The final directions issued on 27 April take effect on 1 April 2027, with the previous framework remaining operative until then. Earlier recognition can make an emerging problem more visible while the bank still has choices about pricing, capital and loan management. It also puts more weight on assumptions about borrowers, collateral and the economy. The rule will work best when investors and supervisors can understand why provisions changed and whether the same evidence would produce a similar result across comparable portfolios. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning · Business Standard on the final provisioning framework

The horizon changes as risk changes

Under the new framework, a loan can require a provision before a missed payment makes it visibly impaired. The directions distinguish 12-month expected credit losses from lifetime expected credit losses and require the longer horizon when credit risk has increased significantly, subject to their terms. Twelve-month expected loss is the portion of lifetime losses associated with defaults possible over the next twelve months. It should not be read as a measure of cash shortfalls incurred only within one year. The transition between horizons can have a material accounting effect even before a default occurs. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning

Suppose an illustrative ₹100 crore portfolio has a two per cent probability of defaults associated with the first horizon and loss severity of 40 per cent. The simplified product is ₹0.8 crore. If a later deterioration triggers a lifetime probability of eight per cent with the same assumed severity and exposure, the illustrative amount is ₹3.2 crore. Actual calculations require expected timing, scenarios, exposure at default and discounting, among other requirements. This example isolates the effect of the horizon. It shows why a change in the bank’s assessment can affect profit and capital before collections fall by a similar amount. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning

Forward-looking means the scenarios have to be explained

A lender’s estimate can change because borrowers have become weaker, because the lender changed the weight assigned to an adverse scenario, or because the composition of the portfolio changed. These are different mechanisms. The directions require multiple scenarios and probability weights determined using evidence and judgement as appropriate. A disclosure that only reports the net increase in provisions leaves outsiders unable to tell whether the loan book deteriorated or the bank became more cautious about the same loans. Reconcile the effects of new loans, migrations between risk categories, recoveries, write-offs and model changes where feasible. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning

The effect on credit can arrive before the accounting deadline. Banks may improve data, tighten lending standards or change pricing while preparing for transition. That can improve risk recognition. It may also make it harder for borrowers whose recent performance looks weak despite a viable business. A rise in rates or decline in new lending should be analysed alongside evidence on applications, borrower quality and the bank’s funding costs. A shortfall in data can be costly if it causes lenders to treat similar risks differently or to rely on conservative assumptions that are difficult to test.

The case for earlier recognition and its limits

The strongest argument for the change is that a lender should account for credible signs of losses before they are fully realised. Earlier recognition gives owners, regulators and bank managers more time to respond. The strongest objection is that several banks can raise provisions at once when the outlook worsens, potentially reducing willingness to lend at a difficult moment. Avoiding that effect altogether would require giving up some information about risk. The relevant question is how the banking system manages the recognised risk with capital, pricing and borrower support, and whether the models distinguish a temporary shock from lasting deterioration. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning · Business Standard on the final provisioning framework

The transition arrangements deserve separate attention. A bank can face a change in reported retained earnings because it applies the new methodology to an existing book, even if its borrowers’ circumstances did not change that day. The RBI sets out how transition impacts are measured and how eligible amounts may be phased for regulatory capital under the specified schedule. Read opening effects alongside subsequent provisions on new or deteriorating exposures. Comparing accounting profit before and after the change without that reconciliation could confuse a change in measurement with a change in performance. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning

One useful exercise would hold the loan portfolio fixed and show how a plausible change in the economic scenarios alters the provision. A second would hold the scenarios fixed and show the effect of borrowers moving between risk categories. The first isolates sensitivity to the model and the outlook. The second gives more information about deterioration in the existing book. Neither comparison predicts realised losses, but both help readers establish what changed. A lender that publishes the reason for a large adjustment is easier to assess than one that reports the adjustment as an isolated figure. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning

There is a distributional issue in model error. A lender may have much better data on larger firms and salaried households than on smaller businesses with volatile receipts. That can create larger uncertainty and conservative assumptions for the second group. Track how often decisions are corrected when additional information becomes available and whether estimates improve as the lender collects reliable evidence.

What to look for in the first disclosures

Compare reported risk migrations, provision coverage, changes in scenario assumptions and realised recoveries over time. Look for differences between otherwise similar exposures, and consider whether the underlying borrowers or the methodology explain them. Earlier warning would be valuable if it improves the bank’s response without causing unjustified differences in access to credit. Repeated large model adjustments that cannot be reconciled with portfolio performance would weaken confidence. The most informative first report will show how the bank reached its estimates and where the uncertainty remains. RBI’s 2026 directions on asset classification and provisioning · Business Standard on the final provisioning framework

excerpt.rendered: The RBI’s final rules move commercial banks towards forward-looking provisioning from April 2027. The transition will show how banks distinguish deteriorating risk from temporary stress.

title.rendered: India’s capital goods surge is a reason to test the investment recovery

content.rendered:
India’s March industrial figures give grounds for optimism about equipment demand and less reason to declare a broad private investment recovery. The quick estimate puts industrial production 4.1% above March 2025, down from the 5.2% February quick estimate. Capital goods rose 14.6% and infrastructure and construction goods 6.7%, while consumer non-durables grew 1.1%. Those categories describe the kinds of goods produced. They do not identify who bought them or how much of the output is already being used. The policy question is whether equipment and materials are flowing into a wider set of productive projects that can continue without a public spending surge. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release · Reuters, 28 April

The largest percentage increase is not necessarily the largest contribution

The index uses fixed base weights for different categories, so their contributions depend on their weights and their previous levels as well as their growth rates. The March table gives capital goods a weight of about 8.22%. Its index rises from 136.3 to 156.2. Multiplying the 19.9-point increase by the category’s weight and dividing by the previous March aggregate index of 166.3 gives a contribution of about 0.98 percentage points. The infrastructure and construction category has a weight of about 12.34%. Its index rises by 14.4 points, implying a contribution of about 1.07 points on the same calculation. The figures are approximate because the published indices are rounded. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release

The two categories thus account for roughly half the 4.1% overall gain, even though the categories’ base weights sum to only about one-fifth. That is a more useful description of March than a claim that all factory activity accelerated. The manufacturing index grew 4.3%, and 14 of its 23 industry groups recorded positive year-on-year growth. Basic metals, motor vehicles and machinery were the largest positive industry contributors in the release. These are useful signs of breadth in some segments. They still allow for weaker conditions among smaller suppliers or producers of goods bought frequently by households. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release

The weakness in frequently purchased goods was consequential precisely because that category is larger. Non-durables carry about 15.33% of the base weight, almost twice the capital goods weight. Their index rose from 149.0 to 150.6, contributing about 0.15 points to headline growth using the same calculation. That shows why a strong equipment reading can dominate the month without representing the typical factory or household. The growth rate for the entire financial year was also 4.1% in this vintage, but that annual average reflects a different mix of months. It cannot be used to infer that the composition of demand was steady throughout the year. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release

Track the buyer before calling it a private investment cycle

A factory can increase production of equipment for several reasons. Private businesses may be installing new production lines. Public agencies and state enterprises may be purchasing machinery or commissioning works. Export orders can absorb output. A manufacturer can also produce ahead of sales, temporarily increasing inventories. The same industrial production reading is consistent with all four. Orders, dispatches, imports of equipment and corporate capital expenditure can narrow the range of explanations. Look for repeated orders across sectors, actual installation and an increase in the use of existing capacity. An increase in output accompanied by rising unsold stock tells a weaker story than equipment delivered to new sites. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release

Capital goods can also have uneven spillovers. A large infrastructure project creates orders for steel, construction machinery and transport. It can relieve a bottleneck and make investment more attractive for firms that would otherwise have paid more to ship goods or secure reliable inputs. It may create little immediate demand for the goods produced by businesses selling to low-income households. A 1.1% increase in non-durables is consistent with subdued growth in that part of industry. It is not a direct measure of household consumption, which includes services, imports and goods produced outside the measured establishments. The two figures can signal an uneven expansion without settling what is happening to purchasing power. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release

There is a serious case for expecting private investment to follow public works. Firms often wait until a port, transmission line or road is usable before committing funds, so the early demand naturally comes from public construction. The strongest evidence for that argument would be private orders and actual investment rising after identifiable bottlenecks are removed. The weaker claim is that any large order for machinery necessarily reflects private firms responding to strong final demand. A buyer can bring forward a replacement or comply with a deadline without expanding capacity. The return on a project depends on its use after installation, not on the fact that equipment was produced for it. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release · Reuters, 28 April

Production and profitability can move in opposite directions

The March figures cover a period in which energy and shipping costs became more uncertain. A producer can keep output high by drawing down inventories or fulfilling earlier contracts at lower margins. That is resilient production in the short run. If costs persist and customers will not accept higher prices, the business may defer its next investment. Firms with access to hedging or suppliers on several routes can absorb a shock more easily than a supplier dependent on one imported input. Comparing physical production with costs, margins and working-capital requirements helps show whether the increase can persist. It is especially important for industries where a rise in sales volumes can tie up more cash before payments arrive. Reuters, 28 April

A comparison with electricity makes the measurement problem concrete. Industrial electricity output rose only 0.8% in the same release, while manufacturing rose 4.3%. The two series have different coverage, and power demand also responds to weather, households and other users. One month’s gap cannot show that factories became more efficient or that the industrial figure is overstated. It can, however, guide a cross-check. Examine plant-level electricity use or industrial demand by state where the data are available, then compare those patterns with output in power-intensive industries. A consistent increase across sources deserves more weight than one indicator on its own. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release

Policy should account for these differences in exposure. A firm holding confirmed orders for profitable projects may need short-term finance if energy or freight bills are paid before its customers settle. A producer accumulating unsold stock faces a demand problem that a credit line may postpone rather than solve. If both apply for support during the same shock, an aggregate production figure provides little basis for treating them alike. Lenders should distinguish verified orders and receivables from inventory that is rising because sales are weak. In turn, policymakers should watch whether producers draw additional credit for delivered orders and repay when those orders are settled. That provides a more direct test of whether financing is the constraint.

What would make the recovery durable

Watch equipment orders, investment spending, project commissioning and capacity utilisation over several releases, including utilisation among smaller firms supplying large projects. Where possible, separate public contracts, exports and private domestic orders, and distinguish new capacity from replacement purchases. Check the stock of unsold goods and real earnings as well. If private orders broaden, projects are completed and consumer demand firms, March will look like an early sign of a more balanced expansion. If the gains remain concentrated in a few publicly supported categories while margins and household sales weaken, the safer judgment is that investment remains uneven. The capital goods figure deserves attention because it identifies a promising part of the economy. The next step is to establish what is paying for it and whether that demand will last. MoSPI’s March 2026 industrial production release · Reuters, 28 April

excerpt.rendered: March factory data show strong capital goods and infrastructure output alongside weak non-durables. The evidence for a durable private investment cycle depends on where the goods went.

title.rendered: India’s rural roads programme should pay for reliable journeys

content.rendered:
Finishing a bridge on a rural route can create more value than upgrading several additional kilometres of road. The Cabinet on 18 April extended Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana-III, which upgrades routes from rural habitations to markets, secondary schools and hospitals. It revised the outlay to ₹83,977 crore from ₹80,250 crore. The case for continuing the programme is strongest where an incomplete link, weak bridge or seasonal interruption still makes the journey unreliable. Delhi and the states should judge projects by the trips that become possible at an acceptable cost. Kilometres completed are useful for monitoring construction and incomplete as a measure of access. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · PMGSY-III programme guidelines

Fix the part of the network that sets the cost of the journey

The extension gives roads in hills and roads and bridges in plains until March 2028, with hill bridges given until March 2029. The Cabinet decision allows tendering of certain works already sanctioned and permits the sanction and award of 161 pending long-span bridges on already sanctioned alignments, at an estimated ₹961 crore. The ₹3,727 crore increase in the overall outlay is about 4.6% of the original allocation. That is a revision to the programme envelope. It should be kept separate from the eventual incremental spending on the bridges and from the value of the work already completed. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III

A missing crossing can determine whether all the adjacent spending is useful. A road that ends at a river a vehicle cannot cross in the monsoon is effectively two separate links. Completing the crossing can shorten the whole trip or allow a bus operator to run a schedule through the year. This is why a project should be ranked by the journey it improves and the availability of other routes. Extending a high-quality road that already has a good alternative may be worth less than making a shorter, unreliable route usable. Appraisals should include detours, waiting times and closures, alongside normal running times. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · PMGSY-III programme guidelines

For illustration, suppose a crossing saves ₹200 on each of 15,000 freight trips a year. That is ₹30 lakh in annual freight savings at existing volumes. Separately, 1,000 regular passengers each making 30 round trips a year could save 20,000 hours in total if each round trip becomes 40 minutes faster. At an assumed ₹75 per hour, that adds ₹15 lakh in time savings. These are illustrative figures, before maintenance, safety or gains from trips that would not otherwise occur. They show how a shorter route can be evaluated even when the project carries few kilometres. Use local counts and values of time for a real appraisal.

The worked example can be carried into the investment decision. If the ₹45 lakh annual benefit lasts ten years and is discounted at an illustrative 8%, its present value is about ₹3.02 crore. The appraisal would deduct construction and maintenance costs and add any independently estimated safety or access benefits. A shorter closure-free life or benefits that accrue only in the dry season would reduce the estimate. New trips can add benefits as well, but they should be valued using evidence of what travellers are willing to pay or save, rather than assuming every new journey is worth the full time saving. The assumptions should be visible before the project is selected.

A road expands options and changes where work happens

A study by Sam Asher and Paul Novosad uses eligibility thresholds in an earlier rural roads programme to estimate the effect of new connections. It finds a shift out of agricultural work, with limited evidence of large short-run gains in village income, assets or agriculture. One interpretation is that the road made it easier to take work outside the village. That is a gain for some households and a reason to keep local enterprise outcomes separate from residents’ earnings. The evidence comes from new connections under an earlier programme. Upgrading a link that is already used can have a different effect. The study is useful because it challenges the assumption that every road will raise output in the place where it is built. Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

The benefits can be uneven within a village. A farmer with saleable surplus and access to a truck can benefit immediately from more buyers. A household that sells little output may gain more from lower bus fares, access to health care or the chance to take paid work in a nearby town. A paved road does not guarantee a scheduled vehicle. Where there is little competition among operators or traffic is too thin, travel costs can fall less than engineering estimates suggest. In those cases the missing complement may be a regular service, usable loading space at the market or a safe route to the pickup point. A monitoring survey should ask who uses the route and who still cannot. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

Maintenance determines whether the benefit persists

The strongest case for extending the construction programme is that stopping halfway through a network can waste earlier investment. There is also a strong argument for moving maintenance up the list. A bridge approach that washes out or a road surface that becomes unsafe can recreate the very detour the project was built to remove. The programme’s guidelines provide for routine maintenance through the initial contracts and address subsequent responsibilities. The policy question is whether funds and inspections are available when those responsibilities fall due. A state that can afford a new link but cannot preserve access on existing roads may get a better return from repair and drainage than from another upgrade. PMGSY-III programme guidelines · ILO study on rural road maintenance

Market access can also alter bargaining. When a grower can get a perishable crop to two wholesale markets instead of one, the local buyer has to compete with a credible outside option. That can raise the farm-gate price even if the farmer rarely changes buyer. The opposite is possible for a local trader protected by the cost of entry, or for a village shop now facing competition from larger markets. Those distributional effects can be tested by recording price differences for comparable grades, transport charges and the number of active buyers before and after a link opens. This offers a clearer measure of integration than the amount spent on the road. Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

For the same reason, the benefit calculation needs a life-cycle cost. A cheap construction bid can become an expensive route if it requires frequent resurfacing or prolonged closures. Spending more on drainage or a more durable crossing may be economical in a flood-prone area. A useful procurement score would report construction cost, scheduled maintenance, expected renewal and the number of days a route is likely to remain open under realistic weather. Publishing actual closures and maintenance payments would make it easier to detect a contractor or design that wins on price while imposing costs on travellers after completion. PMGSY-III programme guidelines · ILO study on rural road maintenance

Measure access after the work is finished

Measure journey times and prices to the specific markets, schools and hospitals the projects are meant to serve, including during the monsoon. Record days closed, bus frequency, freight charges and emergency travel times. Compare routes where the missing link is completed with similar routes that are still waiting, checking whether their pre-completion trends were comparable. Track residents who find work outside the village as well as businesses that open inside it. A rise in reliably completed trips, at lower total cost and with maintained roads, would justify prioritising similar projects. A programme that hits construction targets while journeys remain seasonal would need to change which links it funds and how it maintains them. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

excerpt.rendered: The extension of PMGSY-III gives India time to complete critical links. Its returns depend on year-round travel to markets, schools and hospitals, including after construction ends.

title.rendered: India’s small-city loan guarantee should reward a credible second loan

content.rendered:
The best test of a municipal loan guarantee is the loan a city can get after proving it can repay the first one. The housing ministry has launched the operational guidelines for the Urban Challenge Fund and its credit repayment guarantee. The Cabinet’s February decision set out a ₹5,000 crore guarantee scheme to help eligible smaller cities and urban local bodies in hilly and North-Eastern states access market finance. A guarantee can fill a gap when a lender lacks a record of a city’s performance. It can also allow a weak borrower to postpone a problem. The terms for the next borrowing help distinguish those cases. Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines · Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund

A smaller guarantee can test the original rationale

The Cabinet description provides cover of up to ₹7 crore or 70 per cent of the first loan, whichever is lower. After successful repayment, the corresponding second limit is ₹7 crore or 50 per cent, whichever is lower. The ₹7 crore cap matters. On an illustrative first loan of ₹10 crore the guarantee would cover up to ₹7 crore, leaving at least ₹3 crore outside the guarantee. On a ₹20 crore first loan, the same cap is equivalent to 35 per cent. On a ₹10 crore subsequent loan the percentage limit brings maximum cover down to ₹5 crore. These figures describe the maximum face amount of cover under the stated rules. Recoveries and payout conditions determine the actual losses. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines

For the lender, a guarantee can reduce expected loss without improving the borrower’s ability to generate cash. Its economic value is strongest where the city has a feasible way to pay but the bank has little evidence on payment behaviour, financial controls or performance over time. The first loan can produce that evidence if timely repayment comes from the stated source. If the lender is repaid through an unexpected state rescue, a good repayment statistic may reveal less about the city’s capacity. Record the source of payments, cash reserves drawn down and any extra transfers made to meet the schedule.

A guarantee shifts risk to a wider balance sheet

Suppose 100 eligible cities each have a ₹10 crore loan with maximum first-loan cover of ₹7 crore. The face value of that illustrative exposure is ₹700 crore. If five of the loans default and a full ₹7 crore guarantee is paid on each, the gross cash payout is ₹35 crore before recoveries. This is a stress example, with assumed defaults and no estimate of the programme’s likely losses. Defaults can be correlated when the same state delays transfers or construction costs rise across several towns. That is a reason to report concentration by state, revenue source and project type as well as total guarantees issued.

The April announcement distinguishes ₹90,000 crore earmarked for projects, ₹5,000 crore for project preparation and capacity building, and ₹5,000 crore for the guarantee sub-scheme. These instruments tackle different constraints. A first-time borrower may need help preparing audited records, understanding its own cash flow and specifying a service before any lender can evaluate it. A guarantee applied at the end of that process can overcome uncertainty the lender cannot resolve. Applied in place of preparation, it can protect the lender while leaving the city with an asset it cannot operate on the planned terms. Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines · RBI’s chapter on municipal own revenue

The case for insuring genuine public-service risk

A small city can face borrowing costs that reflect unfamiliarity or a limited lender market even when its finances are sound. A guarantee can widen competition, lower rates and help a city bring a worthwhile project forward. The strongest objection is that a lender with substantial protection may do less scrutiny, or that only cities expecting difficulty choose the guarantee. Leaving some risk with the lender helps, but how much matters depends on the shape of the loss-sharing and recovery terms. A programme can compare the pricing and participation of lenders with and without protection for similar borrowers and project types. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · PRS review of the February Cabinet decision

City residents should also be able to see the repayment source before the project is committed. A service charge, property-tax allocation and state payment put the burden on different people. For a low-income household, a higher basic-service charge may outweigh part of the improvement the project delivers. An identified budget subsidy can protect access if the city or state can credibly fund it. Leaving the shortfall unspecified makes it easier to approve the investment and harder to keep the service available once repayments begin.

Timing matters for the lender and the city. A grace period can help when construction precedes revenue, but interest that accrues during a delay is still a cost. Before a loan is approved, estimate who pays if procurement takes longer or the asset opens partway through a billing year. A plausible project can appear to default if the debt schedule assumes cash arrives sooner than the service can produce it. Reporting construction and payment dates together would reveal whether problems come from poor revenue forecasts or a mismatch between finance and project delivery.

The transition to a second loan should be evaluated for cities that applied and were turned down as well as those that obtained a guarantee. Otherwise, the observed borrowers will be the group lenders already found most promising. Compare application terms and track whether initial rejections can be resolved with better accounts, stronger transfers or a redesigned project. That helps distinguish an information problem from a genuine inability to repay.

Follow the borrowers after the first transaction

The published record should follow applications, rates, maturities, project completion, actual repayment sources and access to subsequent loans. A second loan on improved terms and with less guarantee cover would support the case that the programme is building credit histories. If rates stay high or borrowers need an equivalent public backstop again, identify whether the constraint is lending competition, erratic municipal revenue or the project itself. Financial inclusion for cities has succeeded when it widens the set of services they can sustainably deliver. A first disbursement is only the beginning of that test. Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines · Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund

excerpt.rendered: A first municipal borrowing can be hard even for a viable project. The new guarantee will prove its value if a city builds a repayment record and can later borrow with less protection.

title.rendered: India’s March jobs data show why participation deserves equal billing

content.rendered:
India’s March labour survey gives more reason to watch participation than to dwell on a two-tenths rise in unemployment. The national unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above rose from 4.9% in February to 5.1% in March. Over the same period female labour-force participation fell from 35.3% to 34.4%, and the share of rural adults working fell from 56.3% to 55.5%. These are monthly survey estimates, with room for seasonal and sampling variation. They are nevertheless a useful warning about what the headline can miss. If people who need work stop looking, the unemployment rate can improve at the same time that their opportunities worsen. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin · March PLFS bulletin and methodology · Moneycontrol on the March survey

The denominator determines the story

Under the survey’s current weekly status approach, the labour-force participation rate measures the share of the population in the labour force. The worker-population ratio measures the share employed. The unemployment rate is the share of the labour force that is unemployed. The three are linked. Multiply participation by one minus the unemployment rate to obtain the employment share, up to rounding. The weekly reference period makes the measure responsive to recent conditions. It can classify a person as working after a small amount of qualifying activity, so it should be read alongside hours and earnings when the question is whether people can make a living. March PLFS bulletin and methodology

A numerical example shows why the distinction matters. Take 1,000 adults, of whom 560 are in the labour force and 28 are unemployed. The unemployment rate is 5% and 532 are working. If ten unemployed people stop searching without finding work, the labour force falls to 550 and unemployment to 18. The measured unemployment rate falls to about 3.3% even though 532 people still work. The employment share stays at 53.2%. Conversely, a rise in unemployment can be consistent with an improving economy if new entrants begin looking for jobs before finding them. The March survey cannot establish that either example caused the monthly change. It shows why all three indicators belong together. March PLFS bulletin and methodology

In the published national figures, overall participation fell from 55.9% to 55.4%. Applying the February unemployment rate to the March participation rate gives an implied employment share of about 52.69%, compared with about 53.16% in February. Applying March’s higher unemployment rate then brings the implied share to about 52.57%, close to the published 52.6% after rounding. On that ordering, roughly 0.48 percentage points of the decline comes from participation and about 0.11 from the unemployment rate. This is an accounting calculation using rounded aggregates. It cannot show that particular workers dropped out or establish why the proportions changed. Its policy implication is narrower. A response aimed only at people counted as unemployed would miss most of the movement in the employment share, so a fuller diagnosis should ask what happened to entry, exit and hours. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin

The rural and urban readings suggest different movements. Urban unemployment edged up from 6.6% to 6.8%, while the urban employment share slipped only from 47.0% to 46.8%. Rural employment fell by 0.8 percentage points, a larger change than the urban one.
