title.rendered: India’s GDP revision puts factory output and input costs on a better footing

content.rendered:
The biggest gain from India’s new GDP series is a better way to tell whether a factory produced more or merely earned a wider margin. On 27 February the National Statistical Office shifted the base year from 2011–12 to 2022–23 and released a second advance estimate of 7.6% real growth for 2025–26. The previous estimate was 7.4% on the old series. That difference combines a new method and more information. It says little by itself about which parts of the economy have changed. The more consequential revision is how the statistics convert current-price receipts and costs into real value added, and how much direct evidence they now have about enterprises that are outside the listed corporate sector. NSO’s February GDP release · MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables · Reuters, 27 February

Separating output prices from the prices of inputs

Value added is the value of gross output less the value of intermediate inputs used to make it. A factory’s selling prices can move differently from what it pays for energy, components and materials. When the price of steel, imported chemicals or fuel changes, applying one price index to nominal value added can mistake part of a price movement for a change in production. In the new GDP series, the NSO uses double deflation in manufacturing and agriculture industries where specified, and volume or single extrapolation elsewhere. Double deflation converts output and intermediate consumption to constant prices separately before taking the difference. Its accuracy depends on the quality of both price series. NSO’s February GDP release · MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables

Consider a factory with output worth ₹100 and intermediate inputs costing ₹60 in the base period. Its value added is ₹40. In the next period, suppose it sells the same quantity and uses the same volume of inputs. Its selling prices rise by 5% and the prices it pays for inputs fall by 10%. Nominal output becomes ₹105 and nominal inputs ₹54. Dividing the resulting nominal value added of ₹51 by the output-price index of 1.05 would imply real value added of about ₹48.57, more than 21% above the original ₹40. Deflating output and inputs separately gives ₹100 and ₹60, leaving real value added at ₹40. The figures are illustrative. The example shows how the change can matter particularly in industries where intermediate purchases are large relative to what the firm adds. MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables

There is an economic gain in the example. The plant earns a wider nominal margin and can spend or invest more if its costs stay lower. The change in its purchasing power and profitability is a different object from its volume of production. A firm may use the margin to hire or install equipment later, but the value-added estimate should not assign that output before it happens. Conversely, an energy shock can compress nominal margins even when physical production rises. For fiscal and monetary analysis, look at the separate effects on real activity, selling prices, profits and tax receipts.

Better evidence on small firms makes the aggregate more informative

The revised series draws on the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises and the Periodic Labour Force Survey where applicable. It also incorporates more granular GST and other administrative data. This helps because the relationship between formal firms and informal firms can change. A listed manufacturer may benefit from scale, finance and access to organised buyers when smaller suppliers are struggling. Using the large firms as a proxy can miss that divergence. Direct surveys of the unincorporated sector can improve the estimate of its level and growth. The remaining questions are survey coverage, lags, and how the statistical office treats changes in reporting or shifts between organisational forms. NSO’s February GDP release · MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables

GST records are useful for a different reason. They can give a closer view of reported transactions in the registered economy. An increase in reporting can reflect higher output, an increase in prices, a change in compliance or a business moving into the tax net. Formalisation may improve working conditions or allow a firm to borrow, and those gains are worth measuring. They do not all appear as newly created physical production in the quarter when a firm starts filing. To separate the channels, compare administrative turnover with survey counts, employment and volume indicators in the same industry. The revised series is strongest when those sources cross-check one another. MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables

A higher growth rate can coexist with a smaller current-price economy

The new release puts nominal GDP in 2025–26 at ₹345.47 lakh crore and in 2024–25 at ₹318.07 lakh crore, an increase of 8.6%. The January first advance estimate on the old base put current-year GDP at ₹357.14 lakh crore and the prior year at ₹330.68 lakh crore. The new level for the current year is about ₹11.67 lakh crore, or 3.3%, smaller than the old estimate, even though the growth rate is higher. A change in the base period for constant prices cannot by itself account for a difference in current-price estimates. Updated data and methods also change the measured level. The gap is important for ratios whose numerators, such as public debt or spending, are measured separately in rupees. NSO’s February GDP release · NSO’s January first advance estimate

The figures also answer different timing questions. The new series puts real GDP growth at 7.8% in October–December, after 8.4% in July–September on the same series. Reuters described this as a deceleration. That is compatible with faster growth in October–December than in the same quarter a year earlier, as reported by the ministry. The baseline for one comparison is the previous quarter’s year-on-year growth. The baseline for the other is the year-on-year rate in the corresponding quarter of an earlier year. Analysts should specify the comparison instead of using the change in base year as evidence that the economy either accelerated or slowed. NSO’s February GDP release · Reuters, 27 February

Publish a bridge that researchers can reproduce

The strongest argument for confidence in the revision is that more direct surveys and separate price treatment address identifiable measurement problems. The strongest reason for caution is that several changes happened at once. Better inputs do not tell users how much of a given revision came from a deflator, a new enterprise estimate or late data. Parallel tables for overlapping years, sector-level contributions and eventually a documented back series would let independent researchers isolate the changes. The NSO has provided comparisons between vintages for recent years. The evidence that would build further confidence is that the revised sector estimates track independent physical output and survey indicators more consistently across expansions and downturns. That is a better test of the statistical change than the direction of the first headline revision. NSO’s February GDP release · MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables

Changes in the composition of growth are worth more attention than the two-tenths change in the annual estimate. A revised estimate of manufacturing value added can change which sector appears to be driving the expansion. Its implications for jobs depend on which industries account for the change and whether they are adding shifts, employing more workers or producing more per worker. A sector that now appears larger in measured GDP can still face weak hiring. For the same reason, the real investment series gives more policy information when read alongside capacity utilisation, employment by industry and the balance sheets of smaller firms. NSO’s February GDP release · MoSPI’s methods and comparison tables

The near-term implication is to keep the old and new estimates as distinct vintages in any model. Re-estimate fiscal ratios using a consistent nominal denominator and check whether a relationship estimated on old sector volumes still holds when new data become available. For economic policy, the questions are whether real production is growing, whether firms are investing and whether households see a gain in employment and purchasing power. Better national accounts can make those questions easier to answer. They remain separate questions.

excerpt.rendered: The new GDP series makes a substantive change to the measurement of real value added. Better prices and data improve the diagnosis, and the revisions need a transparent bridge.

title.rendered: The US tariff reset changes India’s bargaining position

content.rendered:
An Indian exporter can face a lower US tariff this week and still become less attractive to an American buyer. The US Supreme Court held on 20 February that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorise the challenged tariffs. The administration ended those duties and imposed a new 10% surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act, effective 24 February, with exemptions. For India, the immediate benefit is a lower additional charge on some covered goods. The loss is that a broad surcharge can erase the relative advantage India hoped to secure in a country-specific agreement. Delhi should use the change to negotiate more predictable access, with the comparison made product by product. US Supreme Court opinion, 20 February · US order ending the IEEPA tariffs · Section 122 proclamation and exclusions

The promised rate and the duty collected have different legal bases

The February bilateral framework said the US would apply an 18% reciprocal tariff on originating Indian goods under Executive Order 14257, including products such as apparel, footwear and some machinery. The joint statement described a framework for an interim agreement. The administration’s subsequent termination order ends the collection of the relevant IEEPA duties. The new proclamation instead imposes a temporary 10% additional charge for 150 days under Section 122, subject to its exclusions. The administration discussed an increase to 15%, the statutory ceiling under this authority, but the published proclamation that took effect specifies 10%. An importer must distinguish what was negotiated, what has been discussed and what customs actually collects. US–India joint statement on the interim framework · US order ending the IEEPA tariffs · Section 122 proclamation and exclusions · Reuters on the surcharge taking effect

The surcharge also sits alongside ordinary tariffs and other trade measures. The proclamation generally adds the surcharge to other duties but provides that it will not stack on the portion of an import subject to Section 232 tariffs. It also lists excluded products. Firms should therefore model the full US tariff line, applicable sectoral duties and country of origin. A $100 shipment does not universally cost $110 at the border. There can also be freight, fees and contract terms that determine which party pays the duty. A negotiator who describes the change as a single new tariff for all Indian exports risks making the wrong comparison in exactly the sectors that matter most. Section 122 proclamation and exclusions

A lower duty can leave India with less of a price advantage

Consider a covered product with a customs value of $100 and assume identical ordinary duties and freight across suppliers. Compare a hypothetical 18% additional rate for India with 20% for an alternative origin. On the same value, the duty-inclusive amounts would have been $118 and $120. Under a common 10% surcharge they are both $110. India has $8 of relief at the border in that comparison, and the competitor has $10. The Indian supplier has lost the $2 relative advantage that would have helped it keep the order. These comparator rates are illustrative. If a competing product is exempt, or carries a different ordinary duty, the gap changes again. US–India joint statement on the interim framework · Section 122 proclamation and exclusions

The converse can be just as important. An Indian producer that was paying a higher rate than rivals may gain relative ground when the gap narrows. A buying office usually has several ways to respond. It can demand a lower factory price, renegotiate its own retail price or shift the next order to another supplier. How much of the tariff relief stays with the Indian factory depends on the buyer’s alternatives and on whether the supplier can insist on keeping its dollar price. A producer with reliable delivery, a certified factory and short lead times can bargain more effectively than a supplier selling an interchangeable product at a thin margin. The potential gain is therefore as much a question about who has options as about the tariff schedule.

Uncertainty changes the order even before duties change again

The 150-day limit creates a mismatch with commercial decisions. An importer placing a seasonal order may care about the duty when goods enter the US, not the rate when the purchase order is signed. A supplier deciding whether to add a production line needs a longer horizon still. A short-lived reduction can help existing orders while doing little to unlock investment. Contracts can allocate the risk through price-adjustment clauses, but the supplier with the least bargaining power may still end up holding the inventory if a buyer can defer or cancel. Reuters reported that India postponed a planned trip by its negotiators after the ruling. That pause makes sense if the price and legal basis of the bargain have changed. Section 122 proclamation and exclusions · Reuters on the postponed talks

The strongest argument for pressing ahead quickly is that a written deal can reduce uncertainty about product exclusions, documentation and future access even when the temporary headline rate is lower. Suppliers may value knowing the tariff and origin rules for a season more than they value a few extra weeks of a lower rate. This is a reason to keep negotiating. It is also a reason to evaluate the terms against a realistic alternative. If the bilateral deal leaves an Indian product facing more than comparable suppliers for little additional certainty, its benefit to that product is small. If it provides durable access for a labour-intensive product whose rivals have stronger terms today, the value can be substantial even if the tariff is positive. US–India joint statement on the interim framework · Section 122 proclamation and exclusions

Use a product-level test for both negotiations and relief

Delhi should build a list of products where the new regime materially changes the relative US duty, and combine it with evidence on employment, export margins and the ability to sell elsewhere. Textile, leather and other factories do not experience a tariff uniformly. A firm whose order is delayed may need bridging credit. A plant whose buyers have shifted permanently may benefit more from product adaptation and access to another market. A tariff headline alone cannot tell a bank which case it is financing. Comparing confirmed orders, cancellations and realised prices by product and destination would help target assistance and avoid paying firms whose US sales were never at risk. US–India joint statement on the interim framework · Reuters on the postponed talks

The investment test is especially demanding for smaller suppliers. A buyer can switch origins for an order without changing the location of its own assets. A factory deciding whether to invest in dyeing capacity or a new production line may be committing capital for years. In that case, lower tariffs for one season do little to improve the investment case unless the buyer makes a credible commitment to future orders. The best negotiating gains are therefore those that reduce the risk of an abrupt change in conditions during the life of the investment, including clear rules and workable transition periods.

Trade data should also distinguish values from quantities. If exporters cut dollar prices to keep buyers, shipment value can fall even while units shipped hold up. If duties push American buyers to accelerate arrivals, a strong month can borrow orders from the next. The cleanest evidence would compare Indian and competing shipments of the same tariff line, control for seasonality and look for persistence after the shipping window closes. Where data allow, track products covered by the surcharge separately from exempt products. A rise in orders concentrated in the lines where India gained relative access would strengthen the case that the policy change helped. Section 122 proclamation and exclusions

India’s bargaining position improves when US buyers depend on suppliers they cannot readily replace. It weakens when access turns on a temporary tariff that changes for everyone. The next agreement should be judged by the stability of entry conditions, by the relative price faced by an American importer and by actual orders for Indian producers. A broad tariff cut this week gives some firms welcome relief. A lasting competitive advantage depends on whether those firms can quote with confidence and keep a larger share of the orders that follow.

title.rendered: A higher collateral-free limit moves the small-business credit test to cash flow

content.rendered:
India’s higher collateral-free threshold for micro and small enterprise loans can help viable firms without property to pledge. The outcome will depend on whether lenders can assess those firms’ cash flows and manage losses. The RBI’s February amendment requires banks not to accept collateral security for covered MSE loans up to ₹20 lakh and takes effect for relevant loans sanctioned or renewed from 1 April 2026. It also allows banks, subject to internal policy and a firm’s track record and financial position, to dispense with collateral up to ₹25 lakh. These changes affect security for a loan. They do not guarantee that any applicant receives one. RBI amendment to the micro and small enterprise lending directions · RBI’s summary of the collateral-free lending amendment

Collateral performs two jobs

Collateral can reduce the lender’s loss if a loan fails and can affect which applicants seek finance. It can also exclude a business with reliable receipts whose owner has little acceptable property. Requiring security may be administratively easier than working out whether a small firm’s accounts and orders support repayment. Removing the requirement can improve access when the lender has other evidence of viability. Where lenders lack that evidence, the change can lead to smaller approved amounts, stricter cash-flow criteria or higher prices. Track those responses together with the number of loans originated. RBI amendment to the micro and small enterprise lending directions · RBI’s summary of the collateral-free lending amendment

Consider two otherwise comparable illustrative loans of ₹15 lakh. Assume a five per cent probability of default over a defined horizon and a loss of ₹4 lakh if the bank can recover much of the secured loan. Expected loss in the simplified example is ₹20,000. If recovery on an unsecured loan leaves a loss of ₹9 lakh, expected loss becomes ₹45,000 at the same default probability. The ₹25,000 difference is not a rate recommendation and ignores timing, costs and guarantees. It shows why a lender needs either better screening, different pricing or another way to manage recoveries. The probability itself can also change as the pool of borrowers changes.

The better screen is a business test

A loan for inventory can be assessed against the firm’s normal sales cycle, buyer concentration and the terms on which it pays suppliers. A machine purchase calls for a longer view of operating cash and the costs of keeping the asset productive. A lender can examine payment records, invoices and bank flows where the firm can provide them. It should allow for seasonality and temporary interruptions. A pattern of regular receipts is useful, though it does not by itself establish profits or the ability to make a payment during a weak period. Viable younger firms may need a way to demonstrate the economics of an order or expansion without a long record.

Requiring sophisticated records from every applicant can reproduce exclusion in a different form. A firm operating partly in cash can have a sound business and limited conventional evidence. Other firms may generate digital turnover while facing low margins and slow collections. A credible underwriting process distinguishes those cases rather than treating all cash transactions as weak or all digital sales as strong. Check whether staff can explain the basis for a lower loan amount or a rejection. That information can help the borrower improve its application and the regulator see which constraints remain binding.

Watch what happens around the threshold

One risk is that lenders cluster loans just below ₹20 lakh even when the firm needs somewhat more. An applicant could receive cheaper or easier access to the first portion of funding while having to finance the rest elsewhere. The firm’s effective cost then depends on both loans and the timing of each. A distribution of sanctioned amounts can reveal bunching, but interpreting it requires comparing the amounts firms asked for and the available alternatives. Some concentration near the threshold may reflect a genuine demand for those loan sizes. RBI amendment to the micro and small enterprise lending directions

The strongest argument for a higher limit is that security requirements can lock capable first-time borrowers out, even when a lender could assess and manage the risk. The strongest qualification is that a guarantee or a different lending rule can reduce one financing obstacle without improving a weak business’s prospects. The useful comparison is how lenders treat applicants with similar expected repayment but different access to assets. A rise in approvals for previously excluded viable firms, with sustainable terms and manageable losses, would show that the change reached the intended margin. RBI amendment to the micro and small enterprise lending directions · RBI’s summary of the collateral-free lending amendment

An additional question is which uses of credit benefit. Working capital for a confirmed order may be easier to assess than an investment with an uncertain return. If banks expand primarily the first category, the reform could improve routine finance while leaving the capital expenditure constraint largely intact. Report loan purpose and maturity alongside approvals. Compare whether a firm that previously borrowed informally now receives enough bank credit at the right time to carry out its plan. The number of new loan accounts is useful only in conjunction with the amount and conditions on which the money arrives.

Because the change applies to new sanctions or renewals from April, an evaluation should follow cohorts from the relevant decision date and allow for the time needed to see repayment. RBI amendment to the micro and small enterprise lending directions

A credit-access test that can distinguish the outcomes

Follow applications, approval rates, pricing, sanctioned amounts, time to disbursement, first-time borrowers and later repayment. Compare loans just below and above relevant thresholds cautiously because firms and lenders can adjust the requested amounts. It would also help to separate first-time applications from renewals, where a bank may already know the borrower. If approvals rise among viable firms without a sharp deterioration in terms or performance, the change has widened access. If loans become smaller or more expensive while approvals barely move, the next task is to identify whether screening, guarantees or another part of the lending process is limiting results. RBI amendment to the micro and small enterprise lending directions · RBI’s summary of the collateral-free lending amendment

title.rendered: India’s AI compute subsidy should be judged by who gets to use it

content.rendered:
India has a case for subsidising access to computing power for AI. A university lab or a small firm can have a promising project and too little capital to reserve the machines it needs. The public programme can lower that barrier. At the India AI Impact Summit on 17 February, the government said it would add 20,000 graphics processing units to the 38,000 already available under the initiative. That is a planned increase of about 53%. The test is how many credible projects get usable computing time on terms they could not otherwise obtain. A larger inventory can help. So can allocating the existing machines better. MeitY’s 17 February summit announcement · IndiaAI compute backgrounder, 17 February

Count usable computing hours

The Cabinet approved the ₹10,371.92 crore IndiaAI Mission in March 2024. Its compute pillar envisaged 10,000 or more GPUs through a public-private partnership and a marketplace through which users could obtain computing services. The outlay is for the wider mission, which also covers areas such as skills, data and startup finance. Comparing that entire figure with the GPU count would give a misleading cost per machine. The relevant public cost of the compute service includes the subsidy actually paid for usage and any financial commitment for capacity that remains idle. Those are the figures to compare with the volume and quality of access delivered. Cabinet approval of the IndiaAI Mission, March 2024 · IndiaAI compute backgrounder, 17 February

A count of GPUs treats very different machines as if they were interchangeable. Memory, the connection between processors, and the ability to reserve several together affect which jobs can run. A team adapting an existing model might need a modest amount of computing spread over several weeks. A larger experiment may need a cluster available at the same time. Both can encounter a shortage even when some capacity is idle. The market can have spare time on one type of machine and a waiting list on another. Publish available and used accelerator hours by hardware class, together with waiting times for different reservation sizes. That would reveal a constraint a headline count cannot. IndiaAI compute backgrounder, 17 February · MeitY’s 17 February summit announcement

The government’s summit backgrounder cites ₹65 per GPU-hour for available capacity. Use that as an illustrative rate. A project renting 32 GPUs for 200 hours uses 6,400 GPU-hours and pays ₹4.16 lakh in accelerator charges, before storage, networking, taxes or staff time. If only 70% of those reserved hours produce useful work, the effective accelerator cost is about ₹93 per useful GPU-hour. A team able to interrupt its job or debug on smaller machines has room to reduce that bill. A research group facing frequent failures or forced to book capacity in larger blocks may pay much more per completed experiment. The price schedule matters alongside the nominal hourly rate. IndiaAI compute backgrounder, 17 February

The subsidy should change who can attempt a project

Access can be undersupplied where a useful experiment has benefits that its sponsor cannot fully charge for. A language dataset, a public evaluation benchmark or a tool for a poorly served Indian language can be reused by others. Its developer may struggle to recover the cost through sales alone. A fixed allocation of compute can help a team demonstrate enough progress to attract funding or show that the project is unworkable before it spends more. The first decision should be whether the intervention changes what can be attempted. A discount on jobs that a well-capitalised company would have run anyway mostly transfers money to the user. Cabinet approval of the IndiaAI Mission, March 2024

The strongest case for granting access to larger teams is that some useful work genuinely needs scale. An experienced team can make productive use of a large cluster and produce a tool that many smaller firms use. Splitting every award into tiny allotments could therefore waste the ability to run certain experiments. A marketplace can accommodate both needs. Give newcomers short initial allocations and reserve a pool for larger, time-bounded requests evaluated against published criteria. Releasing follow-on time against verifiable milestones makes it possible to support ambitious projects without making permanent commitments based on the strength of an application alone. Cabinet approval of the IndiaAI Mission, March 2024 · MeitY’s 17 February summit announcement

There is also a case for keeping much of the service commercial. If subsidies are available at a single low price regardless of demand, high-value users can be crowded out by those willing to reserve time they may never need. Giving commercial users a way to pay for priority while protecting access for approved research helps manage that tension. Cancellation rules and scheduling that can reassign unused reservations can recover hours without buying more machines. Competition among providers can improve service if applicants can take their data and workloads to another provider at reasonable cost. Contracts should make portability and billing transparency part of what the programme buys.

Separate infrastructure from the cost of deploying a useful service

The summit discussion has included a common AI platform for small businesses. A shop, exporter or manufacturer will judge such a service by whether it improves a task at a reasonable ongoing cost. Cheap training time can help create a tool, but deployment can still require clean data, integration with existing software and people who can check its outputs. An invoicing tool that needs regular manual correction saves little time. A language interface that works in demonstrations but performs poorly in a local dialect may generate more support calls. The public return depends on how the tool performs outside the team that built it. Evaluation should include usage by firms after any introductory support ends. The Indian Express’s summit coverage · Cabinet approval of the IndiaAI Mission, March 2024

There are costs outside the budget too. Operating capacity requires dependable electricity, network connections and sites able to support cooling. A location with spare grid capacity at relevant hours can accommodate new demand more easily than a constrained location that needs network upgrades. The public compute programme can limit waste by procuring capacity in stages and asking providers to report energy per completed workload where measurement is comparable. The point is to compare different ways of delivering usable capacity, including access to existing machines, before paying for more. Additional demand on a power system should be considered alongside the gains to researchers and firms.

An evaluation can start with the applications themselves. If awards use a published scoring threshold, compare applicants just above and below it whose proposals and funding look similar. Follow both groups over the same period to see whether an award shortened the time to complete an experiment, increased the chance of finishing it or merely replaced a cloud bill the team would have paid anyway. Where access is allocated through other means, a staggered rollout or a lottery among equally ranked applications can provide a useful comparison. Count the costs paid by teams as well as the public subsidy. That would give a more credible estimate of additional work than dividing the total number of awards by the available machines.

Publish evidence on who gains access

The government should report active users and usage by type of organisation, the share going to first-time users, median wait times, used and reserved hours, subsidy per completed project and how concentrated awards are among recipients. Track whether supported projects go on to produce reproducible evaluations, tools that independent users adopt or commercial products that can sustain their own compute bills. An increase in genuine first-time access, with shorter queues and repeat use of the resulting tools, would strengthen the case for expansion. High utilisation dominated by a few teams that already had market access would weaken it. If the constraint turns out to be staff, data or adoption, the next rupee may do more there than on another processor. Cabinet approval of the IndiaAI Mission, March 2024 · IndiaAI compute backgrounder, 17 February
