title.rendered: Clean production only helps an exporter if the emissions can be verified

content.rendered:
An Indian producer can operate a lower-emissions plant and still fail to translate that advantage into better terms in Europe. The EU’s definitive carbon border regime began on 1 January. Its December implementing rules specify how embedded emissions are calculated and how declared values are verified. If a producer’s information is incomplete or fails the applicable verification requirements, the buyer may have to use a default value. The commercial gap can therefore reflect both how goods were produced and what the exporter can credibly prove about their production. European Commission’s December start-date notice · EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations · EU implementing regulation on verification

The definition of the product comes before the number

The calculation rules set boundaries for production processes and attribution to goods. A producer first has to determine which data belong to the relevant installation, process and product. A total for an entire company may include unrelated output. A site-wide electricity or fuel number can also be inappropriate if several products have to be allocated their share of emissions. For complex goods, relevant precursor emissions can matter. The useful record follows the production and input documentation needed for the particular covered good, with calculation choices that can be checked later. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

The availability of a reported number and its suitability for compliance are different questions. A firm may have an internal estimate for energy management that uses a broader boundary or a different factor from the applicable rules. The importer needs a figure calculated on the required basis, with the appropriate verification. Default values give a structured route where actual values are unavailable or not used. The applicable default can depend on the good and circumstances, so it should be identified from the operative rules rather than guessed from a country average. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations · EU implementing regulation on verification · EU implementing regulation on default values

When it makes economic sense to pay for verification

Assume an exporter’s usable actual value would be 1.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of product and the applicable default would be 1.7. Over an illustrative shipment of 1,000 tonnes, the difference is 500 tonnes of embedded emissions. At an assumed carbon price of €70, the gross value of that difference is €35,000 before relevant adjustments, phase-in rules and contract terms. This is a comparison of assumed values rather than a claim about a specific product, installation or bill. It gives an exporter a way to estimate how much verified data could be worth to a buyer. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations · EU implementing regulation on default values

Suppose preparing and verifying the records costs €12,000. That cost could be worthwhile if enough of the gross difference actually affects certificates and the exporter can retain some of the value through price, volume or customer retention. It is less attractive if the order is small, the true intensity is close to the default or the buyer cannot use the information. The same records may support repeated sales, making the fixed cost easier to recover. The commercial decision should use the expected value across likely orders, not just the savings on a single hypothetical consignment.

The buyer also needs confidence in the timing

A factory may be able to calculate the number and still deliver it too late for the importer’s planning and reporting. Contracts should establish who supplies precursor data, who arranges verification and when a material change in sourcing or production has to be disclosed. This can affect competition within India. Large plants may spread the fixed cost of compliance across greater volume. Smaller firms may need common expertise or reliable services for measurement and reporting. That does not remove the need for facility- and product-specific evidence where the regulation requires it. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations · EU implementing regulation on verification

The strongest argument for accepting defaults initially is that the effort to verify actual emissions can be disproportionate for a small trial order. A default gives the parties a common starting point when a supplier cannot yet assemble reliable records. The drawback is that it can obscure a real emissions advantage and give buyers a reason to switch to suppliers whose documentation is easier to use. A sensible test is to compare the two valuations before committing to a substantial verification expense, then start with products where both the emissions difference and the prospect of repeat trade are credible. EU implementing regulation on default values · EU implementing regulation on verification

The division of work between firms matters because precursor data can be difficult to assemble after a batch is sold. A manufacturer buying material from several producers should retain the information needed to relate those inputs to the products actually shipped. If a purchasing manager changes suppliers to avoid a production interruption, the emissions file must also reflect the change where relevant. Recordkeeping should be part of the ordinary production and purchasing system. A spreadsheet assembled at the end of the year can be expensive to reconcile and may provide weak evidence about a particular order. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

There is a useful distinction between documentation that helps verify a claim and investment that lowers emissions. Better measurement can reveal an existing advantage without changing output or fuel use. It can also identify the production stage where an emissions reduction would matter most. An exporter should account for both effects when considering new equipment. A reduction that cannot be demonstrated to the buyer may still cut energy costs, while a reporting improvement can have immediate commercial value without reducing emissions. Tracking the effects separately makes the investment comparison clearer. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations · EU implementing regulation on verification

What would show that reporting is changing competition

Track whether buyers are asking for verified installation data, whether they use the information, the difference between actual and default values and changes in contracts or sourcing. Compare results across suppliers with similar production but different reporting capacity. If credible lower-emissions producers can retain buyers or obtain better terms, verification is transmitting a real production advantage. If records are repeatedly rejected or delivered after commercial decisions have been made, spending on cleaner production alone will not explain the observed outcome. The near-term opportunity is to make the environmental difference legible in a contract. EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations · EU implementing regulation on verification

excerpt.rendered: The EU’s definitive carbon border regime makes production records commercially valuable. Firms should compare the cost of proving actual emissions with the cost of being assessed on defaults.

title.rendered: Cheap farm credit is most valuable to farmers who can get it before sowing

content.rendered:
A farm loan at 4% can be transformative if the money arrives before sowing. For a farmer waiting on a bank approval when seed and fertiliser bills fall due, the advertised rate can matter very little. The Reserve Bank’s 13 January circular continues the Modified Interest Subvention Scheme for short-term loans through the Kisan Credit Card. It sets out a subsidised lending rate of 7%, an additional benefit for timely repayment and an overall eligible amount of ₹3 lakh. The policy priority should be getting timely formal finance to farmers who still borrow informally or have to cut back on inputs. Increasing the subsidised ceiling can help existing borrowers. It does less for farmers who are outside the system. RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy · NABARD rural financial inclusion survey results

The limit in the circular is the operative one

The February 2025 Budget speech announced an increase in the interest subsidy limit from ₹3 lakh to ₹5 lakh. The January circular governing 2025–26 describes benefits on up to ₹3 lakh. It also provides a ₹2 lakh ceiling for allied-activity credit under the relevant rules and gives crop borrowing priority within the overall limit. A higher sanctioned card limit and a higher amount qualifying for the subsidy are two separate decisions. The RBI’s own illustrations include sanctioned Kisan Credit Card limits above ₹3 lakh and apply benefits only to the eligible portion. Banks and borrowers should work from the circular when calculating this year’s subsidy. Union Budget 2025–26 speech · Cabinet decision on the interest subsidy · RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy

Take a farmer drawing ₹1.5 lakh for six months, with a constant balance and no fees. At 7%, simple interest is ₹5,250. A 3 percentage point prompt repayment incentive lowers the effective annual rate to 4% and the six-month interest to ₹3,000, a ₹2,250 reduction. On those assumptions, the separately calculated 1.5 percentage point lender subsidy amounts to ₹1,125. That payment helps the lender offer the administered rate. It should be counted separately from the borrower’s interest bill. Actual subsidy calculations follow the dates and caps in the circular, so irregular drawings and earlier repayment change the amounts. RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy

For a farmer buying inputs in the next fortnight, the value of the facility can exceed the saving in interest. An informal loan can be available the same day and can accommodate repayments timed to a particular sale. It may carry a high price or bind the farmer to one trader. A formal bank line that is available reliably can improve the farmer’s ability to shop for inputs and sell output to another buyer. A loan approval that arrives after sowing provides much less leverage. Performance data should therefore include when borrowers first drew the funds, alongside the sanctioned limit and interest rate.

The problem is who gets through the application

NABARD’s 2021–22 financial inclusion survey, analysed by Dvara Research, found that 75.5% of agricultural households reporting a loan borrowed exclusively from institutional sources. The remainder used a non-institutional source for at least some of their borrowing. The denominator is agricultural households reporting a loan. It excludes households that needed credit but never obtained any. The data are from an earlier survey round, so they establish a substantial gap at that time, with no direct estimate of the current gap. For the same reason, the number of cards issued tells us little about eligible households that never applied or whose cards remain unused. NABARD rural financial inclusion survey results · Dvara Research’s survey analysis

The RBI previously raised the collateral and margin waiver for agricultural loans to ₹2 lakh per borrower, effective from January 2025. This can help farmers who have a viable crop plan but lack acceptable security. Screening and documentation still matter. A tenant may be able to establish cultivation through local evidence yet find it difficult to meet a lender’s paperwork requirements. A farmer with existing bank relationships can navigate renewals more easily. The January circular requires Aadhaar authentication and limits subsidy duplication for the same parcel. Those provisions can protect public money. They also make it important to monitor failed verifications and allow errors to be corrected quickly enough for borrowers to plant on time. RBI collateral circular · RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy

A higher subsidy ceiling has a serious case. The cost of cultivating a commercial crop can exceed the eligible amount, especially on farms with more acreage, irrigation or expensive inputs. A grower who has exhausted the subsidy may turn to informal credit for the balance. But the fiscal gain per borrower rises with the size and duration of the eligible loan. An expansion concentrated among borrowers already able to borrow commercially would deliver less additional access per public rupee than an expansion that brings previously excluded cultivators into formal finance. The relevant comparison is between the additional lending each policy produces, including the rate paid on the next rupee, and the subsidy cost. Union Budget 2025–26 speech · RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy

A fiscal comparison can make the trade-off explicit. Suppose one million already eligible borrowers each draw an additional ₹1 lakh for a full year and repay on time. At the present rates, the combined 1.5 percentage point lender subvention and 3 percentage point borrower incentive on that increment would amount to ₹450 crore. The same calculation for half-year drawdowns gives ₹225 crore. These are scenarios under the existing subsidy rates, with assumed take-up, rather than a cost estimate for the proposed expansion. The government could compare the benefit of those higher balances with what a similar sum might achieve in speeding up first approvals, resolving documentation problems or extending the reach of local lenders. RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy · Union Budget 2025–26 speech

Repayment incentives work best when farm risks are recognised

The prompt repayment benefit gives a farmer a reason to repay on time and a lender a way to distinguish ordinary cash-flow management from emerging stress. Farm incomes can also move together after a flood, drought or price collapse. A farmer whose crop has failed can miss the repayment date despite having made sensible decisions. The circular provides for lender subvention on restructured loans after natural calamities and additional relief for severe cases under specified procedures. Transparent and timely application of those rules matters. An unexpected delay in relief can force a farmer to sell assets or refinance at a higher rate before the concession arrives. RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy

The circular also permits eligible small and marginal farmers to receive interest subvention for up to six months after harvest against negotiable warehouse receipts for produce in accredited warehouses. This addresses a specific problem. A farmer who must repay immediately may accept a low price while many neighbours are selling the same crop. A warehouse-backed loan can make it possible to wait. The gain depends on the eventual price, interest, storage charges and deterioration. It also depends on a practical route to an accredited warehouse. In a district with few facilities, aggregation through a credible local organisation can matter more for take-up than a further cut in the nominal rate. RBI’s 13 January circular on the interest subsidy

What the government should measure

Publish application, approval and drawdown data by district and crop season, separating renewals from first-time borrowers. Track time to drawdown, reasons for rejection, failed authentication and the share of borrowers who repay on time without taking another expensive loan. Survey tenant cultivators and other eligible applicants whose experiences disappear from loan registers. An increase in cards accompanied by earlier drawdowns, lower informal borrowing and better access for tenants would support the case for expanding the facility. If balances rise mainly among existing borrowers and the time to secure funds barely changes, widening access should take precedence over raising the subsidised amount. A farm credit policy earns its subsidy when it changes the decision a farmer can make before the crop goes into the ground.

excerpt.rendered: The RBI’s January circular keeps subsidised crop credit at ₹3 lakh. The bigger policy test is whether farmers can obtain usable credit when input bills fall due.

title.rendered: India’s 8% nominal growth estimate leaves the deficit maths largely intact

content.rendered:
India’s first estimate of 7.4% real growth for 2025–26 is stronger than last year’s 6.5% on the same statistical vintage. The 8.0% nominal growth estimate has attracted attention because February’s Union Budget assumed 10.1%. Taken literally, that gap sounds like a large hole in the denominator of the fiscal deficit. The two growth rates start from different estimates of the previous year’s GDP. In rupees, the January estimate of this year’s economy is slightly above the Budget’s. The fiscal risk lies chiefly in what the Centre collects and spends, including how much of its public investment programme it can carry through. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January · Union Budget 2025–26, Budget at a Glance · Business Standard’s fiscal analysis, 7 January

Reconcile the levels before comparing growth rates

The 2025–26 Budget put nominal GDP at ₹356.98 lakh crore, about 10.1% above the then-used estimate of ₹324.11 lakh crore for 2024–25. The National Statistical Office now estimates 2025–26 nominal GDP at ₹357.14 lakh crore and compares it with ₹330.68 lakh crore for 2024–25. The previous year’s base is roughly ₹6.57 lakh crore higher than the one in the Budget arithmetic. The projected level for the current year is roughly ₹0.16 lakh crore higher. The slower growth rate and slightly higher endpoint can therefore be true together. Applying 10.1% to the updated base would create a hypothetical level that the February Budget never used. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January · Union Budget 2025–26, Budget at a Glance

The Budget’s planned fiscal deficit is ₹15,68,936 crore, or ₹15.68936 lakh crore. Holding that borrowing requirement fixed, the old denominator puts the ratio at about 4.395%, and the January estimate puts it at about 4.393%. Both round to 4.4%. This exercise holds the numerator fixed to isolate the statistical effect. It shows why a revised nominal growth rate, by itself, is a poor reason to expect the government to miss its fiscal ratio. A real change in cash receipts or spending can still move the numerator by much more than the revised denominator moves the ratio. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January · Union Budget 2025–26, Budget at a Glance

Nominal growth remains economically important. Dividing 1.08 by 1.074 gives an implied rise in the GDP deflator of roughly 0.6%, using rounded growth rates. That deflator covers the prices of domestic output across the economy, with weights different from the household consumption basket. A government can face subdued growth in taxable turnover even while the volume of goods and services increases rapidly. Equally, strong growth in the activities where tax is actually paid can sustain receipts. The composition of nominal income and spending matters because tax bases and effective rates differ across households, firms and products. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January

The January number is a first advance estimate. The NSO extrapolates previous-year benchmarks using available indicators, including industrial production, listed-company accounts for the first two quarters and crop estimates. Its current-price taxes on products use Budget assumptions alongside available cash-account information. The output estimate and the Budget thus share some inputs, particularly where full-year outturns are still unknown. Treating them as independent confirmations of one another would overstate the evidence. The January release is most useful as a coherent estimate at a given date, with revisions expected as company, government and sector data arrive. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January

The cash accounts are the more immediate fiscal test

Through November, the Controller General of Accounts records Centre net tax receipts at ₹13.94 lakh crore, or 49.1% of the full-year Budget estimate. The comparable proportion a year earlier was 55.9%. Non-tax revenue had reached 88.6% of its estimate, ahead of last year’s 78.3%. Capital expenditure had reached ₹6.58 lakh crore, or 58.7% of its annual estimate, compared with 46.2% a year earlier. Taken together, the figures show a different spending and receipt profile from last year. The cumulative fiscal deficit stood at ₹9.77 lakh crore, or 62.3% of the annual estimate. Controller General of Accounts, November 2025

It would be a mistake to project the deficit from the first eight months using a straight line. Advance tax payments, transfers to states and large non-tax receipts are uneven over the year, as are the dates when projects are paid for. The stronger case for confidence is that some of the shortfall in tax receipts relative to the Budget path can be absorbed by non-tax revenue and by subsequent collections. The weaker version of that argument assumes that every favourable non-tax receipt repeats. For next year’s spending decisions, a recurring tax base provides more room than a receipt that depends on a particular dividend or transaction. Controller General of Accounts, November 2025 · Business Standard’s fiscal analysis, 7 January

The composition of the investment estimate also matters. The NSO puts real gross fixed capital formation growth at 7.8%, up from 7.1% in 2024–25. Real private consumption is estimated to grow 7.0%. The fixed investment measure covers the economy and combines public investment, household capital formation and business investment. The stronger aggregate cannot by itself establish that private firms are starting a broad investment cycle. If public works account for much of the gain, a late-year slowdown in capital payments could remove a source of demand for construction, materials and suppliers. If business investment is broadening on its own, the economy is better placed to absorb more gradual public spending growth. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January · Controller General of Accounts, November 2025

Different sectors are also contributing at different rates. The release estimates real value added in agriculture and allied activities growing 3.1%, while financial, real estate and professional services are put at 9.9%. That divergence can matter for employment and for the taxes that are collected. A city service business and a farming household experience different prices and market conditions, even in the same national expansion. The sector figures are value added at constant prices. They neither measure the distribution of household income nor translate directly into government revenue. They help identify where detailed evidence on wages, profits and sales is needed. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January

Set next year’s assumptions in rupees

A conservative Budget should separate its current-year estimate of the tax base from its forecast of how that base will grow. For illustration, if next year begins from ₹357.14 lakh crore, a nominal growth assumption of 10% implies GDP of ₹392.85 lakh crore. At 8%, the denominator would be ₹385.71 lakh crore. With a hypothetical deficit ceiling of 4.3%, the two assumptions imply borrowing limits about ₹30,700 crore apart. This is a sensitivity calculation, not a forecast for the next Budget. If the lower-growth scenario also reduces tax receipts, the spending choices would tighten by more than the borrowing arithmetic alone suggests. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January

Low inflation brings benefits that the cash accounts do not capture. A household whose nominal pay is steady can buy more if prices are lower than expected. The government may also face slower growth in some procurement costs, and the cost of refinancing debt can respond over time. That is a reason to avoid treating slower nominal GDP growth as a uniformly negative event. It is also why an expenditure cut should turn on the return to the spending. Postponing an unready project may have little economic cost. Delaying payments on productive works that are already under way can be more damaging, particularly for smaller contractors with limited liquidity.

What the next vintage should change

MoSPI says the next annual release will use a new base year. That can alter the historical series and the estimated level of output. Preserve both vintages when assessing which part of the fiscal picture changed. The useful comparisons are revised nominal GDP against the earlier level, taxes collected against the revised tax base, and actual capital payments and project delivery against the spending plan. If net tax receipts strengthen and projects continue to be delivered, the present estimate offers little reason for late-year fiscal retrenchment. If collections weaken and public investment slows, the strain will have come through the numerator and the composition of spending. Those are the numbers to read alongside the growth headline. MoSPI’s First Advance Estimates, 7 January · Controller General of Accounts, November 2025

excerpt.rendered: Comparing the January GDP estimate with the original Budget requires matching the two data vintages. The denominator has barely changed. The pressure is on tax receipts and spending choices.

title.rendered: Sri Lanka’s cyclone recovery needs three different financing plans

content.rendered:
Sri Lanka needs to finance emergency relief, restore basic services and rebuild against future storms. Putting those needs in one spending total can hide the financing gap that matters at each stage. The IMF approved around $206 million in emergency support on 19 December following Cyclone Ditwah. Three days later the World Bank estimated direct physical damage at $4.1 billion. The two numbers describe different quantities. The IMF decision offers immediate balance-of-payments support. The World Bank estimate values damage to assets and provides a baseline for deciding what needs to be restored or replaced. IMF’s emergency financing decision for Sri Lanka · World Bank’s Cyclone Ditwah damage assessment

Damage, loss and public cost differ

A ruined road, house or piece of equipment has a replacement or repair cost. A worker losing income because access is cut faces a loss even if their own house remains usable. Government then has to decide what to finance, from emergency assistance to rebuilding public infrastructure or helping households recover. Its fiscal cost can be smaller or larger than the value of public assets damaged, depending on assistance, financing terms, and whether projects are upgraded for resilience. A physical damage estimate should not be treated as a reconstruction budget or a tally of future economic losses. World Bank’s Cyclone Ditwah damage assessment

Comparing $206 million with $4.1 billion gives roughly five per cent. This is an arithmetic comparison for scale. It is not the share of rebuilding funded, because the numerator is emergency external financing and the denominator is estimated direct damage to assets across sectors. Counting both amounts as funding or cost in the same programme would produce a misleading conclusion. The appropriate accounting separates immediate foreign-currency needs, public spending commitments and the cost of replacing or making safe the assets that will actually be rebuilt. IMF’s emergency financing decision for Sri Lanka · World Bank’s Cyclone Ditwah damage assessment

Relief comes first where waiting is expensive

The first financing plan needs flexible cash for essential services, temporary support and imports that cannot wait for a project appraisal. An extra week without access to a clinic or a reliable road can impose costs that do not appear in the bill to replace a damaged asset. Emergency external funding helps where suppliers must be paid in foreign currency or lost income weakens the country’s external position. Record where the money went and what it restored. Speed has an economic value, especially when an interruption would otherwise cause avoidable harm and longer-term loss of earnings. IMF’s emergency financing decision for Sri Lanka

The second plan concerns restoration. The government may be able to reopen a route or service with a temporary repair before it can complete a permanent project. Paying twice for a service may be sensible if waiting months for the final asset would cost more. A decision should compare the extra cost of the temporary work with the value of the service restored sooner. The risk is that a temporary solution becomes permanent through inertia. A funded maintenance plan and a review date help establish whether the initial repair is still serving its intended purpose.

Long-lived assets need a different appraisal

The third plan should compare rebuilding to the previous standard with investing in a more resilient one. Suppose a road can be restored at a cost of 100 units, while an improved design costs 115. Assume the improvement reduces expected future losses by three units a year for ten years. At an illustrative five per cent discount rate, the avoided losses are worth about 23 units in present value. Under those assumptions, the extra 15 units are worthwhile. The result changes if the design proves less effective, the expected hazard is lower or the road has better alternatives. This is a worked comparison, not an estimate for any Sri Lankan project.

The financing horizon should match that decision. A long-lived improvement can justify financing with a longer maturity where the government can afford the repayment and where the terms reflect the project’s public benefits. Short-term funds can be valuable for reopening a service while creating a poor match if they are the main source for a multi-year rebuild. Grants or concessional terms can improve the comparison. Even then, the fiscal plan needs to show future operating costs and whether debt service rises in years already subject to other commitments. IMF’s emergency financing decision for Sri Lanka · World Bank’s Cyclone Ditwah damage assessment

The case for protecting the stabilisation effort

A serious objection to open-ended reconstruction spending is that it can make debt and inflation harder to control, especially after a crisis. That argues for a defined envelope, transparent procurement and a record of grants and debt raised. The opposite mistake is insisting on the same near-term spending path regardless of the shock. If basic services stay unavailable and taxable activity does not recover, a smaller first-year deficit can create a larger economic cost. The choice should be based on the sequence and quality of the spending and the credibility of financing, with temporary measures identified as such. IMF’s emergency financing decision for Sri Lanka

Household support needs its own measure of coverage. Paying a fixed amount only on documented asset damage can miss renters and informal workers whose homes or earnings are disrupted. A registry tied to loss of access, income interruption and household vulnerability can expose gaps in a scheme designed around property records. Reporting who actually received support and how soon would make the distributional consequences of the financing plan visible. World Bank’s Cyclone Ditwah damage assessment

What a recovery report should show

Publish immediate assistance delivered, restoration times, long-term project costs and funding by source. Match physical progress to services restored, and check whether vulnerable households and regions can actually access support. Show how new foreign borrowing affects future payments. If the early funding reopens services and a separately financed programme rebuilds critical assets with better protection, the emergency response will have helped buy a lasting recovery. If the same commitments are counted repeatedly across announcements, the public will still lack an account of what has been financed and what is left to do. World Bank’s Cyclone Ditwah damage assessment · IMF’s emergency financing decision for Sri Lanka

excerpt.rendered: The World Bank’s damage estimate and IMF’s emergency financing measure different things. Recovery depends on matching immediate relief, restoration and long-term rebuilding to the right funding.

title.rendered: India’s banks can absorb losses. The harder test is keeping credit open.

content.rendered:
India enters 2026 with the strongest bank asset quality in years. The Reserve Bank’s December Financial Stability Report puts gross non-performing assets at 2.2% of scheduled commercial bank advances in September and net bad loans at 0.5%. Its stress tests also leave the major banks above minimum capital requirements in the scenarios examined. That is good news for the economy’s capacity to absorb losses. The harder question is how much credit would still reach households and firms if banks conserved capital and wholesale lenders withdrew at the same time. The distinction matters because an economy can experience a credit squeeze with every large bank still open. RBI December Financial Stability Report release · RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

Start with the right denominator

The report’s 2.2% headline covers scheduled commercial banks in aggregate. Its main macro stress exercise uses 46 banks whose starting gross bad-loan ratio is 2.1% and whose aggregate capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio is 17.1%. In the baseline that capital ratio reaches 16.8% by March 2027. It falls to 14.5% and 14.1% under the two hypothetical adverse paths. The baseline bad-loan ratio is projected to fall to 1.9%. The adverse capital numbers are conditional results from a model. The sample matters, and the 1.9% is an estimate for the future rather than a measure of current loan quality. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter · The Indian Express’s coverage of the stress tests

At the individual-bank level, the RBI finds no breach of the 9% minimum total capital ratio in either adverse macro scenario. Four banks could use part of their capital conservation buffer in the harsher scenario absent fresh capital. That is what a buffer is for. Using it can still make management and investors more cautious, particularly when losses are rising and an equity issue would be expensive. For an industrial borrower seeking a higher working-capital limit, the distinction between breaching the minimum and operating with a thinner buffer matters less than whether the bank will actually renew the line. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

A separate exercise is more revealing about the weaker tail. The RBI applies a single credit shock that takes the sample’s bad-loan ratio from 2.1% to 8.1%. The aggregate capital ratio remains above the minimum, but six banks representing 15% of scheduled commercial banks’ assets would breach it. This result belongs to the single-factor sensitivity test. It is separate from the macro scenarios that leave all 46 above the minimum. A useful reading of both is that aggregate resilience is real and that the distribution of losses can still determine which local credit markets come under strain. Customers of a stressed bank may need time to establish a relationship with another lender. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

An illustration separates the two ways the ratio can move. A bank with ₹10,000 crore of risk-weighted assets and ₹1,710 crore of regulatory capital starts at 17.1%. If provisions and losses reduce capital by ₹300 crore, the ratio falls to 14.1% at unchanged risk-weighted assets. If credit deterioration also raises risk-weighted assets to ₹11,000 crore, it falls to about 12.8%. Conversely, the bank can support its ratio by making fewer new loans or shifting to assets with lower risk weights. These amounts are illustrative, and the RBI’s actual scenario is calculated using bank-level models. The arithmetic explains why a stable ratio can coexist with a reduction in the credit available to a risky but viable borrower.

Where a solvent banking system can still transmit distress

Banks and non-bank lenders serve different borrowers and rely on different funding mixes. A non-bank lender that funds longer loans by rolling short-dated borrowing is exposed to the risk that markets decline to renew it. The lender can then protect cash by slowing originations, including to people who are still repaying on time. A bank that has lent to that company may remain well capitalised while deciding it wants less exposure to the entire segment. The household or small firm that cannot readily substitute a bank loan sees the tightness first. The RBI reports that microfinance and self-help-group lending within the NBFC retail segment contracted over the last two half-years. That makes disaggregated lending indicators worth watching even while the broad NBFC balance sheet looks sound. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

The RBI’s interconnectedness exercise offers a measure of the exposure. It estimates that failure of the private non-bank finance company with the greatest capacity to transmit losses would absorb 3.0% of banking-system Tier 1 capital in its solvency simulation. The analogous result for the housing finance company with the largest impact is 3.6%. Neither standalone exercise takes a bank below the regulatory capital minimum. A joint shock can still behave differently. Several lenders might face the same funding market and sell similar assets into a thin market. Creditworthy borrowers can lose multiple sources of funding at once. A solvency exercise and a liquidity exercise are therefore complementary, and the same institution can look healthy in one and exposed in the other. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

There is also a measurement issue in the reported acceleration of non-bank credit. The upper and middle layers together recorded year-on-year credit growth of 21.3% in September, but the RBI says reclassification of two housing finance companies into the upper layer materially affected the comparison. On a common set of upper-layer institutions, credit growth showed some deceleration. A supervisor assessing whether lenders are chasing volume would get a more informative answer by holding the reporting population fixed and inspecting loans by origination quarter and product. Otherwise a change in the reporting boundary can look like a change in how much credit reached the economy. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

Capital should give lenders room to make distinctions

The strongest case against a tougher supervisory response is that India spent years resolving large bank exposures and rebuilding capacity. Banks now have better aggregate capital and lower bad loans. Excessively defensive lending can deny working capital to firms with sound orders or push households into higher-cost credit. That is a good reason to avoid a blanket restriction. The useful response is to test concentrations and funding dependencies, then ask institutions with concentrated risk to show how they would fund commitments and absorb losses. A large lender with stable deposits, a diverse book and credible loss reserves can keep lending through conditions that warrant caution at a lender reliant on one short-term market. RBI December Financial Stability Report release · RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

Averages also deserve scrutiny when banks are growing rapidly. The bad-loan ratio can decline because existing loans recover or are written off, or because performing balances grow faster than new defaults. The RBI’s half-yearly slippage ratio was stable at 0.7%, with a marginal increase for private banks. Tracking fresh delinquencies and recoveries alongside write-offs and loan growth would show whether the lower bad-loan ratio reflects a better stock of borrowers or merely a larger denominator. Early missed payments by loan vintage are especially useful when new credit has had little time to season. RBI Financial Stability Report, financial institutions chapter

What the next report needs to show

The RBI should track the ability of banks and non-banks to maintain credit to comparable borrowers under stress. Useful measures include unused credit lines, renewal rates, new lending spreads after controlling for risk, the maturity of wholesale funding and the share of capital held by institutions with thin buffers. If isolated losses are absorbed and viable firms can continue to draw and renew facilities, the case for confidence strengthens. If aggregate capital stays high while loan approvals collapse in several exposed segments and wholesale funding becomes more concentrated, the system is transmitting distress even though its solvency indicators remain reassuring. India’s improved bank balance sheets are valuable because they give lenders a chance to keep financing sound activity in a downturn.

excerpt.rendered: The RBI’s December stress tests show ample aggregate bank capital. The economy still depends on how banks and non-bank lenders respond when funding tightens and losses concentrate.

title.rendered: The apple quota is the real test of India’s New Zealand trade deal

content.rendered:
India’s new trade agreement with New Zealand will give an early test of how much agricultural competition Delhi can accommodate. The two countries announced the conclusion of negotiations on 22 December. India kept major dairy lines outside the concessions while agreeing to preferential access for selected horticultural products. The apple quota is worth examining on its own terms. It opens part of the market in a defined season and gives the government a way to observe the effects. Whether consumers gain, and whether the opening is manageable for Indian growers, depends on how the import rights are allocated and what happens to prices at the orchard gate. Commerce Ministry’s announcement, 22 December · New Zealand government’s announcement

The quota starts close to existing shipments

The Commerce Ministry’s factsheet puts current Indian imports of apples from New Zealand at 31,393 tonnes, worth $32.4 million, and imports from the world at roughly 519,652 tonnes. The agreement would start with a preferential quota of 32,500 tonnes, rising to 45,000 tonnes in year six. The first figure is about 6.3% of the factsheet’s total import benchmark and only about 1,107 tonnes above its reported New Zealand volume. New Zealand’s government compares the quota with a lower recent average of its own exports. Those statements can coexist because the reference periods and measures differ. India should evaluate the preference against several seasons of customs data, including the share of New Zealand shipments that previously arrived during the eligible months. India’s December agreement factsheet · New Zealand government’s announcement · New Zealand Apples and Pears’ account of the quota

Eligible apples would face a 25% duty within the quota, against the prevailing 50% outside it, with a minimum import price of $1.25 per kilogram and a window from April through August. Those conditions matter more than the headline percentage cut. At the $1.25 threshold, and assuming the same customs value under both rates, the value plus this duty would be $1.56 per kilogram at 25% and $1.88 at 50%, before other charges. The difference is about 31 US cents. If the entire first-year quota used the preference at that price, the gross duty difference on those shipments would be about $10.2 million. The actual revenue effect depends on what would otherwise have been imported and at what value. India’s December agreement factsheet · New Zealand Apples and Pears’ account of the quota

The same factsheet’s import value and tonnage imply an average of about $1.03 per kilogram for the existing New Zealand trade. That aggregate unit value mixes grades, shipment dates and contracts, so a direct price comparison would be misleading. It illustrates a selection effect. Some fruit previously imported at a lower declared unit value might need to sell at a higher price or continue under the prevailing duty. A wholesaler specialising in premium grades may capture much more of the preference than a supplier targeting the lowest-price segment. The quota’s effect should be measured separately for comparable grades and shipment months. India’s December agreement factsheet

A seasonal opening still affects the value of storage

The strongest argument for the window is that apples from the Southern Hemisphere can add supply when fewer Indian apples are coming straight from orchards. A household may get more choice and a grocer may have more reliable deliveries during those months. This could divert trade from other suppliers that continue to pay the full tariff. In that case New Zealand shipments would rise while total imports moved much less. If landed costs fall but comparable wholesale and retail prices barely change, importers, overseas suppliers or retailers may be keeping the tariff saving. That outcome would be consistent with quota rights being scarce or with limited competition downstream. New Zealand government’s announcement · India’s December agreement factsheet

The preferential tonnage also looks modest beside the domestic crop. A US Department of Agriculture field report projects Indian apple production at 2.61 million tonnes in marketing year 2025/26. The initial quota is equivalent to about 1.2% of that projection. This is a comparison of scale, with the quota measured by agreement year and production by marketing year. It says little about the price effect in a particular market. An extra shipment sold into a narrow grade in a weak month can move prices for those sellers, even when the volume is small relative to the national harvest. Local price and stock data should therefore carry more weight than the national ratio in any review. USDA’s 2025 India fruit report · India’s December agreement factsheet

The strongest case for caution comes from domestic fruit sold out of storage. The relevant overlap is with Indian apples available for sale, which includes fruit kept in controlled atmosphere stores after harvest. An orchard’s expected return depends partly on the price that can be realised several months later. Cheaper imports during the storage season could reduce that price, trim the return on storage investment and change what a trader bids at harvest. The effect can reach growers who never see an imported apple in their local market. It can also differ sharply by grade and state. Premium imported apples may compete closely with some stored lots and weakly with other fruit sold in smaller towns.

Even where prices decline, lower margins on storage are only one side of the distribution. Consumers pay for spoilage and handling through the price of fruit. More predictable supply can reduce seasonal price spikes. A defensible opening allows some of that benefit while giving Indian growers a practical way to raise the value of their crop. The announced agricultural productivity plans for apples, kiwifruit and honey can help where the binding constraints are nursery quality, disease management, sorting or loss in transit. The evidence would be higher saleable yields, a larger premium for consistent grades and lower losses for participating growers over several seasons. Commerce Ministry’s announcement, 22 December · India’s December agreement factsheet

Quota design decides who keeps the tariff saving

Allocating rights to firms based on past imports is administratively convenient. It also hands incumbents an advantage when the supply of permits is scarce. A small importer may have a willing supplier and a buyer but no preference to claim. An auction could return some of the quota value to the public, although it would need modest lot sizes and release dates that fit shipping schedules. A first-come system avoids an explicit licence price but can reward firms that can finance early cargoes. Whichever method India adopts, publishing aggregate allocations, uptake and the concentration of rights would let traders and consumers see whether the design encourages entry or entrenches a few firms.

The bargain extends beyond apples. India’s negotiators say most sensitive dairy lines were excluded, while the published outcomes allow narrow access for milk albumins and provide concessions on selected dairy-based food preparations. A broad dairy opening would affect a different market with frequent cash receipts for producers and established cooperative procurement networks. The orchard example supports testing access where the volumes, price floor and season are visible. It offers little basis for extrapolating to all farm products. India’s release also cites a $20 billion investment commitment over 15 years. Firms will invest when projects can earn a return. The investment figure is best monitored through actual project decisions and realised capital expenditure, alongside trade flows. Commerce Ministry’s announcement, 22 December · India’s December agreement factsheet · New Zealand government’s tariff outcomes

What would justify a larger opening

Once the agreement takes effect, customs could publish monthly imports by origin and grade where available, the share entering within the quota and the average customs value. Pair those figures with domestic wholesale prices, comparable retail prices and farm-gate prices for stored apples. Comparing affected months with the rest of the year, and separating unusually large harvests from ordinary ones, would help distinguish import competition from a bumper crop or a storage shock. A falling retail price alongside stable farm-gate margins and stronger domestic grading capacity would make the case for a larger opening. If permits remain concentrated and the consumer price barely changes while growers receive less, the administration of the quota deserves attention before its scale expands. India’s December agreement factsheet

title.rendered: India’s 125-day jobs guarantee will be tested when states run short of funds

content.rendered:
The extra 25 days in India’s proposed rural jobs guarantee are worth having. The more consequential change is who pays for the next day of work after a state exhausts its central allocation. Parliament has now passed the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Bill, which would replace MGNREGA and raise the annual entitlement from 100 to 125 days per rural household. The Bill retains an entitlement to work and an unemployment allowance in specified circumstances. It also changes how the Centre and states finance the programme. Unless the funding rules can respond to a local shock, some of the districts that most need the extra work could face the greatest difficulty providing it. Bill text and financial memorandum · NDTV, 19 December · MGNREGA, section 22

The household’s right and the state’s budget have different limits

Under MGNREGA, the Centre bears the wages for unskilled manual work and up to three-fourths of the material component, which includes the wages of skilled and semi-skilled workers. States bear their share of materials and pay any unemployment allowance due. Under the Bill, the Centre and most states would share programme expenditure within the normative allocation in a 60:40 ratio. The ratio would be 90:10 for the specified north-eastern and Himalayan jurisdictions. The Centre would determine a normative allocation for each state each financial year under rules yet to be prescribed. The state would bear spending above its allocation. The allocation governs who pays. The separate employment entitlement governs what households can claim. MGNREGA, section 22 · Bill text and financial memorandum

Consider a state in the 60:40 group with ₹100 crore of eligible spending within its allocation. It would put up ₹40 crore. If another ₹20 crore of demand comes in and all of it falls above the allocation, the state would pay the full ₹20 crore, raising its total contribution to ₹60 crore. Had that same additional spending qualified for matching funds, the extra state contribution would have been ₹8 crore. The allocation boundary therefore raises the marginal state cost of a rupee of eligible work from 40 paise to one rupee. This simplified example leaves out unemployment allowances and administrative adjustments. The actual amounts depend on the rules and the composition of spending. Bill text and financial memorandum

The Bill’s financial memorandum estimates a nationwide annual requirement of ₹1,51,282 crore for wages, materials and administration, with a central share of about ₹95,692 crore. For comparison, the existing scheme’s Union budget estimate for 2025–26 is ₹86,000 crore. The difference is about ₹9,692 crore in central terms. The two figures have different statuses. One is a nationwide estimate in a legislative memorandum and the other is a budget allocation for the existing scheme. Neither tells us how much money will be available to a particular district in a drought. For that, the allocation formula and the timing of releases matter. Bill text and financial memorandum · Rural Development Ministry’s budget figures

An employment guarantee earns its keep in a bad year

The programme provides insurance because families can ask for work when private incomes fall. A drought can cut days of farm work and increase the number of households seeking public work in the same district. Under the new financing design, the cost of providing additional days can rise sharply just as the state faces other drought-related expenses. A state may still fund the work. It may also postpone project approvals or run out of sanctioned works in the blocks under most pressure. An entitlement that depends on the timing of a supplementary state budget is less valuable to a family that needs income this month. Bill text and financial memorandum

Administrative records cannot show all the work people wanted. The Rural Development Ministry reports 290.60 crore person-days under MGNREGA in FY2024–25 and puts women’s participation at 58.15%. The scale makes implementation at the panchayat level consequential. An offer recorded against a household’s application reveals little about how many days it received, whether the site was reachable or whether it could afford to wait for payment. And if people stop applying after being turned away informally, registered demand can fall while hardship rises. The Bill provides for an allowance where work is unavailable within 15 days under the applicable conditions. A dated receipt for a work request is what lets a worker establish when that clock started. Rural Development Ministry’s FY2024–25 figures · Bill text and financial memorandum

Women and households without land may have fewer options when local work is unavailable. A worker who can travel for seasonal employment can look farther afield. A worker who must stay near home to care for children or older relatives has a narrower choice. In a randomised evaluation of improvements to the public employment programme in Andhra Pradesh, Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus and Sandip Sukhtankar found gains in private-sector wages and employment that accounted for most of the income gains. That result applies to the reform and labour markets studied. It illustrates why a credible public-work option can affect the terms of private work as well as the incomes of people on a government muster roll. Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar, Econometrica

The case for cost sharing is strongest when it improves project selection

A credible argument for state co-financing is that states and panchayats choose much of the work and should face some of its cost. If a project produces little of lasting value, a funding rule that puts nearly all of the wage cost elsewhere can weaken the incentive to choose a better one. The Bill prioritises categories such as water security and resilience to extreme weather. A village that builds and maintains a useful water-harvesting structure gets income support today and a potentially more productive farm economy later. Predictable annual allocations can help panchayats plan those works and buy materials in advance. That case is strongest when transfers reward useful completed assets and well-documented demand. Shifting the full cost to a state at the allocation boundary does little by itself to distinguish good projects from bad ones. Bill text and financial memorandum · Rural Development Ministry’s introduction of the Bill · The Indian Express analysis of the Bill

There is a similar trade-off in the Bill’s requirement that states designate a total of 60 days for peak sowing and harvesting when scheme work will pause. Farmers have a legitimate interest in finding labour when delaying a harvest would destroy value. A calendar that fits one crop or district can still close the public option in another place where work is scarce. It can also weaken workers’ bargaining position during the period when farmers most need them. The Bill provides for geographic differentiation in the notifications. Fine-grained calendars and a usable route to revise them when the rains move would matter more than administrative uniformity. Bill text and financial memorandum · The Indian Express analysis of the Bill

Make the funding rule respond to the same shocks as the guarantee

The Centre could start with an allocation formula that incorporates rural population, poverty and exposure to agricultural shocks, as well as past work. A formula built mainly on historical spending risks rewarding states that already had the staff, project pipeline and payment systems to turn requests into work. It can then give less to states where low spending reflected poor access in the first place. The Bill allows the Centre to consider relaxations on a state’s recommendation in cases of natural calamity and extraordinary circumstances. Published triggers for supplementary financing, linked for example to notified drought and a documented jump in work requests, would give states a clearer basis for preparing projects before their regular allocation runs out. Bill text and financial memorandum

The test is what happens after a bad harvest. Report work requested, offered and actually worked by block and month, along with the time from request to assignment, the time from work to payment and unemployment allowances due and paid. Compare districts with similar weather shocks before and after the change, paying particular attention to states nearing their allocations. Independent household surveys can check for unregistered demand. If work expands in distressed districts and workers are paid promptly without a rise in low-value projects, the case for the new model strengthens. If demand rises while days worked stall at funding boundaries, a higher statutory entitlement will have been undermined by the financing rule.

excerpt.rendered: Parliament has approved a longer rural jobs guarantee. Its value as insurance against bad harvests and weak labour markets depends on whether work can expand when a state exhausts its central allocation.

title.rendered: India’s new cess puts the use of earmarked revenue under scrutiny

content.rendered:
The new Health Security se National Security Cess Act should be judged by two things. The first is whether its capacity-based assessment improves collection. The second is whether the spending it is meant to support can be traced through the budget. The Gazette published the Act on 16 December after assent on 15 December. It provides for commencement by a separate notification. The design initially concerns specified pan masala production and measures liability through machinery or processes. For India’s fiscal federalism, the choice of a cess matters because the Constitution treats specific-purpose cesses differently from taxes in the divisible pool. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess · Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

The collection argument is about what the government can observe

A tax on reported output depends on being able to observe production or sales. If they are hard to measure, a tax based on installed machinery and rated capacity can give the authority a different basis for assessment. The finance ministry described a structure linked to machine speed and pack weight, with separate treatment of manual processes. Capacity can be easier to verify than every item sold. It can also be a poor proxy for actual production when firms differ in utilisation. Whether it improves collection depends on how reliably the authority can identify installed capacity, idle equipment and changes in the production process. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess

Consider two illustrative producers paying the same ₹10 lakh monthly levy because they have comparable taxable capacity. If one sells 500,000 units and the other 250,000, the levy is equivalent to ₹2 and ₹4 per unit respectively before considering their other costs. Those numbers are assumed and do not describe the Act’s rates. The example shows why a capacity levy can penalise low utilisation while giving a producer little additional tax cost on a further unit within the same category. It may therefore alter decisions about machine size, shifts and how production is organised. That behaviour belongs in any estimate of expected revenue.

The tax-sharing question concerns the denominator

Under Article 270, specified cesses levied for specific purposes are excluded from distribution through the divisible pool. Suppose an illustrative Union tax collection is 100 units, of which ten are outside the pool, and ignore collection costs. At a 41 per cent state share of the remaining 90, aggregate devolution is 36.9 units. If 15 units are outside the pool with the same gross revenue and state share, it is 34.85 units. The arithmetic is hypothetical and does not forecast the new cess’s receipts. It shows why the composition of taxes can affect devolution while the stated sharing percentage is constant. Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

The effect on a state’s ability to finance a service depends on where the money ultimately goes and under what conditions. Union spending may benefit residents in several states, including in ways that are difficult to allocate by place. A transfer through the divisible pool gives states a different degree of discretion from expenditure tied to a specific purpose. The two can both be valuable. A credible comparison should show which services the revenue supports, how it is allocated and whether it finances spending in addition to what was already budgeted. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

The strongest case for a dedicated levy

A levy with stated purposes can give legislators and the public a reason to check whether the proceeds support those activities. A capacity assessment can improve enforceability in a sector where reported output is unreliable. That case is strongest when the budget shows collections and related appropriations and when administration can cope with variation across firms. Earmarking can also reduce flexibility or give the appearance of new funding when a department uses dedicated receipts to replace ordinary revenue. A review should compare what changed against a credible spending baseline. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess

The economic incidence is not fixed by the name of the taxpayer. Producers can try to pass on costs through prices, absorb them in margins or change the products and volumes they offer. Demand and competition determine how far each is possible. The relationship between the levy and the public-health objective should therefore be assessed with evidence on prices, output and use of the proceeds. The effective tax per unit can vary across producers even under the same machinery rule, which makes the distribution of the burden an empirical question.

The capacity schedule also creates boundaries between production methods. If liability jumps at a given rated speed or pack configuration, a manufacturer can change its investment or product mix even where underlying demand is unchanged. The enforcement agency should report how many establishments are in each band and how that distribution changes after the measure takes effect. A change in the mix may be an ordinary commercial response. It is also a reason to distinguish higher assessed capacity, higher effective tax rates and improved compliance when explaining collections. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess

Fiscal transparency also requires a baseline that includes ordinary budget funding for the stated purposes. Suppose a department would have spent 100 units from general resources and now spends the same amount using 20 units of dedicated revenue. Twenty units have a traceable source, while the financed activity has not grown. If expenditure rises to 120 on a comparable basis, there is more evidence of additional funding. This example holds other budget choices constant.

What a transparent first account would show

Report the taxable capacity assessed, collections, administrative costs, disputes and the variation in actual production relative to that capacity. Separately reconcile the amounts collected with budget authorisations and spending on the purposes stated in the law. Report how the composition of Union taxes affects the share of gross collections available for devolution. If collection improves and the financed activities can be identified, the design has a stronger case. If it changes the tax base while the destination and additionality of spending remain obscure, that is where parliamentary scrutiny should focus. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess · Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

excerpt.rendered: A capacity-based levy can make revenue easier to assess. Its public-finance case also depends on how spending is authorised and what the levy means for tax sharing.

title.rendered: Pakistan’s stronger reserves still need a test against payments coming due

content.rendered:
Pakistan’s December IMF reviews have reduced immediate financing pressure. The next test is whether the country can keep reserves growing when external payments are due and temporary support has to be renewed. The IMF Board completed reviews under the Extended Fund Facility and the Resilience and Sustainability Facility on 8 December, allowing access to around $1 billion and $200 million respectively. These funds can buy time for adjustment. The improvement will be more durable if recurring export and transfer receipts can cover a larger share of external payments, and if less of the remaining gap depends on short-term borrowing. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan · IMF December staff report on Pakistan

The stock of reserves improved from a low base

The IMF’s December figures put gross reserves at $14.5 billion at the end of FY2025, up from $9.4 billion the previous year. That is an increase of about $5.1 billion, or 54 per cent on the rounded numbers. The same table puts the current account at a surplus of 0.5 per cent of GDP in FY2025 after a deficit of 0.6 per cent in FY2024. Those improvements predate the December release of funds. They help explain why near-term pressure has eased, while neither statistic establishes that all dollars in the reserve stock are freely available to cover an unexpected outflow. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan

A reserve stock can rise for several reasons. Export and remittance receipts can exceed the amounts the private economy needs. A sovereign can borrow abroad and add the proceeds to reserves. A creditor can extend a deposit that might otherwise have to be repaid. Each can improve the near-term position. The debt created, the rights associated with particular assets and the timing of payments determine how much insurance the increase provides. To assess that insurance, look at usable assets and scheduled gross financing needs, alongside the headline stock and the maturity structure of financing. IMF December staff report on Pakistan

Suppose a country reports $15 billion in gross reserves and expects $6 billion of payments to fall due within a year. If $4 billion is credibly refinanced, the net amount it must find for those maturities is $2 billion. If only $1 billion is renewed, the amount is $5 billion. This stylised example excludes new current-account flows, other payments and valuation effects. The gross reserve number is identical in both cases. The change in rollover conditions alters the buffer that can be used for imports, intervention or other commitments. A reserve target without a refinancing calendar leaves that exposure invisible.

A current-account improvement can arise from different adjustments

A current-account surplus supported by stronger export volumes and resilient remittances gives a different outlook from a surplus driven by suppressed imports. In the second case, demand for intermediate goods and equipment may return when activity recovers, increasing the need for dollars. The IMF reports a primary fiscal surplus of 1.3 per cent of GDP in FY2025 and expects growth to increase from an estimated 3.0 per cent to a projected 3.2 per cent in FY2026. A stronger recovery would be welcome. Assessing its financing requires looking at what that growth imports and whether domestic producers can earn additional foreign exchange. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan · IMF December staff report on Pakistan

The distribution of the adjustment matters. When access to foreign exchange is uncertain, small importers can struggle to finance inputs even where large firms find alternatives. Workers can bear the cost through fewer hours or delayed investment. Depreciation can improve exporters’ competitiveness while raising prices for food, fuel and inputs with little immediate domestic substitute. An external strategy that leans heavily on import compression can stabilise the aggregate in the short run at a cost to the capacity that would help earn dollars later. Sector-level import volumes and export performance are better tests of that trade-off than the headline balance alone.

Why bridge financing can be worth taking

The strongest case for official financing is that a country facing a tight maturity schedule may need time to avoid disorderly cuts and make fiscal and structural adjustments. Paying a maturing creditor on time can protect market access and reduce disruption to ordinary trade. An improvement in the quality of the adjustment is a legitimate return on that time. The risk is that each new disbursement mainly finances earlier obligations while the underlying constraints stay in place. A durable strategy should gradually reduce reliance on repeated temporary sources, even if a period of official funding is necessary to reach it. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan · IMF December staff report on Pakistan

The flood-related food-price pressure identified by the IMF also complicates the immediate policy choice. A rise concentrated in affected crops calls for a different response from a broad deterioration in inflation expectations. Tight demand management can preserve confidence in the currency but may add costs for borrowers facing a real supply loss. The choice should be assessed alongside the response of imports, reserves and domestic credit. That is another reason to follow quantities and payment schedules, rather than reading every change in a reserve stock as a change in underlying capacity. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan

The distinction also matters for evaluating partners. A multilateral loan, a commercial bond and a short bilateral deposit can each support the same gross reserve number. Their costs, conditions and maturity dates can differ materially. Publishing the composition of new liabilities, along with a conservative assessment of which rollovers are already agreed, would help distinguish a broadening source of finance from a concentrated dependency. IMF December staff report on Pakistan

What would make the reserve improvement durable

Track the next twelve months of maturities, actual rollovers, the sources of changes in reserves, export volumes and the cost of access to external funding. Compare import changes across fuel, consumer goods and productive inputs. Stronger exports and continued access to funding at longer maturities would improve the judgement. Repeatedly extending short-term obligations while domestic firms struggle to finance essential inputs would make it less favourable. December’s financing matters because it gives Pakistan room to demonstrate which path it is taking. IMF December staff report on Pakistan

excerpt.rendered: The December IMF reviews unlocked roughly $1.2 billion. The durability of Pakistan’s recovery depends on how much foreign exchange it can generate and retain after meeting its obligations.

title.rendered: A Fed cut cannot do the work of financing India’s external deficit

content.rendered:
India should resist the temptation to treat ₹90 to the dollar as a line the Reserve Bank must defend. On 10 December the Federal Reserve cut its policy rate by 25 basis points, and on 11 December the rupee still hit a record low of 90.4675 before closing at 90.3675. The apparent puzzle becomes easier to understand once India’s current account and its financing are considered together. India has been earning more from services and remittances. At the same time, a sharp swing in portfolio flows has made dollars harder to attract. A Fed cut can help at the margin. Durable relief depends on the returns investors expect to earn in India and on the country’s capacity to finance its import bill through a change in global risk appetite. Federal Reserve policy decision · Reuters, 11 December · RBI’s July–September balance of payments

The rate cut and the return on a rupee investment are different prices

The Fed lowered its target range to 3.50–3.75%. The median participant still put the appropriate rate at 3.4% at the end of 2026, the same as in September. The median is an assessment by policymakers under their individual economic assumptions. Investors can price a different path. US Treasury data show the two-year par yield declining from 3.61% on 9 December to 3.54% on the 10th and 3.52% on the 11th. A smaller decline than the quarter-point cut is unsurprising for an instrument that reflects expected short rates over two years as well as a term premium. The figures are daily observations. Establishing what the announcement itself changed would require intraday prices around the decision and the next Indian trading session. Federal Reserve policy decision · December FOMC projections · US Treasury daily yield data

A simple dollar-return calculation shows the size of the currency exposure. Take a hypothetical one-year rupee investment yielding 6.5% and a dollar alternative yielding 3.6%. At an initial exchange rate of ₹90, an investor converts $1 into ₹90 and ends the year with ₹95.85. If the rupee is then at ₹94, the investment converts back to about $1.020, a dollar return of roughly 2.0% before costs. The break-even exchange rate against the dollar alternative is about ₹92.52. A depreciation of about 2.8% over the year would wipe out the initial yield advantage. A fully hedged investor faces the forward rate and trading costs instead. These are assumed investment yields, and the example excludes taxes, credit losses and any change in the price of the security.

The calculation also shows why different investors respond differently. A foreign equity fund can tolerate an adverse currency move if it expects Indian earnings to grow quickly enough. A fund benchmarked to dollar bonds has less room to do so. An importer with an invoice due next week can buy dollars even if it thinks the rupee will recover next year. These buyers and sellers meet in the same currency market on very different time horizons. A decline in Treasury yields improves one part of their arithmetic. It can be outweighed by weaker expected earnings, the need to hedge a payable or a higher premium for holding India risk.

The current account improved as portfolio financing reversed

The RBI’s preliminary July–September balance of payments puts the current-account deficit at $12.3 billion, or 1.3% of GDP, against $20.8 billion and 2.2% a year earlier. The goods gap narrowed only $1.1 billion. Net services receipts rose $6.4 billion, while personal transfer receipts, chiefly remittances, increased $3.8 billion on a gross basis. Net primary income payments rose $3.0 billion, absorbing part of the improvement. A smaller deficit lowers the net amount India needs from financial flows. How that amount is financed can still change dramatically. RBI’s July–September balance of payments

Net foreign portfolio investment moved from a $19.9 billion inflow to a $5.7 billion outflow, a $25.6 billion swing. That is about three times the $8.5 billion improvement in the current account. Net foreign direct investment improved from a $2.8 billion outflow to a $2.9 billion inflow. Net external commercial borrowing and non-resident deposits also contributed less than a year earlier. The RBI records a $10.9 billion draw on reserves on a balance-of-payments basis, against an $18.6 billion addition in the comparable quarter. That measure strips out valuation changes. It helps show how the financing mix changed, even though it cannot establish which transactions moved the rupee in December. RBI’s July–September balance of payments

The quarter’s figures and the daily market tell us different things. Reuters reported on Thursday that foreign investors had sold nearly $18 billion of Indian stocks so far this calendar year. That figure concerns equities over a different period from the RBI’s quarterly net portfolio number, which covers more than stocks. Nor can either number tell us how much of a given sale was converted to dollars on the day. What the two observations do establish is that the supply of foreign risk capital can vary by much more than the current-account deficit improves. For policy, the maturity and reversibility of financing deserve as much attention as the size of the deficit. Reuters, 11 December · RBI’s July–September balance of payments

Use reserves to preserve a functioning market

There is a respectable case for intervention even if India can absorb a weaker currency. A sharp move can trigger stop orders and cause importers to rush to cover together. Dealers can quote wider spreads or cut the size they are willing to trade, making the cost of a hedge jump well beyond the movement in spot. A manufacturer with dollar debt and mainly rupee receipts can face higher debt-service costs before it can adjust prices.
